You close the laptop at six, but the day does not end. A half-answered email, a client waiting on a figure, a form that is almost finished — they follow you to dinner, into the evening, and sometimes into bed. The work has not stopped; it has simply moved into your head.

For a notary, a fiduciary, a doctor or a small office, the heaviest load is rarely the work itself. It is the open loops — the dozens of small things that are neither done nor forgotten, floating somewhere between "later" and "I must not forget this". A calm five-minute routine at the end of the day can put them down where they belong, so you can actually switch off.

Why the evening decides your morning

Most people plan their day in the morning, when the inbox is already loud and the phone is ringing. But the best plan is made the evening before, while you still know exactly what is open. Two things happen when you close the day on purpose:

  • You stop carrying the list in your head. Once a loose end is written down and given a place, your brain can let go of it.
  • You start tomorrow calm. Instead of re-discovering your own chaos at eight o'clock, you walk in and know the first three things to do.

The five-minute shutdown, step by step

This is not another productivity system to maintain. It is five minutes, at the same time every evening, and the AI does the sorting. You only need a note app, a voice memo or a piece of paper.

Step 1 — Empty your head (three minutes)

Write down everything that is still open. Do not order it, do not judge it, and do not start doing any of it. Just get it out: the email you owe someone, the appointment you must confirm, the invoice that needs checking, the idea you want to keep for tomorrow.

Step 2 — Hand the mess to the AI

Paste the list into your AI of choice — ChatGPT, Claude or a local model — with a simple prompt:

Here is my end-of-day brain dump: [your list]. Sort it into three lists. (1) For tomorrow, in the order I should do it. (2) Waiting on — things where I am waiting for someone else. (3) Parked — things I can decide on later this week. Keep each item short. Do not add tasks I did not write down.

Step 3 — Choose tomorrow's first three

From the "for tomorrow" list, pick the first three. Ask the AI to turn them into three concrete first steps, each small enough to start in under ten minutes. That is your opening move for the morning — decided the evening before, while you were still calm.

A second prompt: the one-line closing note

There is real value in ending the day knowing what actually got done. Before you close, ask the AI to summarise the day in a single calm sentence:

Here is what I finished today: [a few notes]. Write one short sentence that sums up today's progress in a calm, factual tone — no hype, no pressure. I will read it once and then close the day.

One honest caveat

The routine must stay small, or it becomes another open loop. Five minutes, the same questions, then you stop. The AI does not decide your priorities — you do. It only sorts what you already knew and hands it back in a shape you can use. And the data rule is the same as always: for client names, patient details or confidential figures, use a local model or an anonymised version of the list.

The morning feels lighter, because the first three steps are already waiting. That is the whole point: this routine is not about doing more. Filee: A Free File Converter That Never Uploads Your Files

Data protectionDocumentsOffice

A photo arrives from a client’s iPhone, the insurance portal wants a PDF, and the quote has to go out as a Word file. Between those small mismatches sits a familiar reflex: search for an “online file converter”, drag the document onto the first website, download the result. It works — and it quietly sends your file, with everything inside it, to a server you know nothing about. A free tool called Filee does the same job entirely on your own computer.

A small daily problem

File formats are the unnoticed friction of office life. An iPhone saves photos as HEIC, which many older programs refuse to open. A scan sits there as a JPG, but the portal insists on PDF. A client sends an old Word file; the offer has to go back as a PDF. None of it is difficult — but every detour costs minutes, and the tempting shortcut is always the same search box.

Online converters are fast, free and need no installation. The hidden price is the upload: the file travels to whoever runs the website, and you rarely learn where the server stands or how long the copy is kept. For a holiday photo, that hardly matters. For a client’s contract, a payslip or a patient letter, the question looks different.

What Filee does

Filee is a free, open-source converter for Windows, with preview versions for macOS and Linux. You hold the Ctrl key and drag a file onto any free spot on your screen: a small wheel of format icons opens at your cursor, and you drop the file onto the format you want. No program window, no account, no upload.

The list covers the everyday office cases — images, PDF, Word, Excel, PowerPoint, plain text, e-books and archives, more than 240 formats in total. Several files can be converted in one go, and where no direct path exists, Filee chains the steps itself, for example from an older format to a newer one and on to the one you actually asked for. A few special cases borrow well-known helper programs (such as LibreOffice or FFmpeg) the first time they are needed; after that one download, everything runs on your machine again.

Why “stays on your computer” matters in Switzerland

As soon as a file contains anything about a person — a name on a contract, a salary figure, a health detail — it counts as personal data under the revised Swiss Data Protection Act. Self-employed people and small businesses carry the responsibility for what happens to that data, including what their tools do with it. An online converter hands the file to an unknown operator, often outside Switzerland, with no control over storage or deletion. A local converter removes the question entirely: nothing leaves your computer, so there is no third party you would have to trust or check.

Honest limits, and a simple habit

  • Windows 10 and 11 are the stable platform; the macOS and Linux versions are previews. On a Mac, the first launch needs the “Open Anyway” step, because the app is not yet signed.
  • Filee changes formats — it does not edit content. Corrections, signatures and blacked-out lines stay where they belong: with you and your other tools.
  • Keep the original, convert a copy, and glance at the result before it goes to a client. A converter saves time, not the final check.

A file converter will not change your business, and that is fine. But it removes a quiet, recurring risk from the daily routine — for exactly zero francs.

Find Your First AI Task: A One-Week Audit of Where Your Time Really Goes

Planning Focus Productivity

Most Swiss self-employed people don't get stuck with AI because the tools are hard. They get stuck because they can't decide where to begin. There are dozens of small admin tasks, each feels equally urgent, and the quiet worry of picking the wrong one means nothing changes at all.

There is a calm way through this. Before you automate a single thing, spend one ordinary week noticing where your hours actually go. The result is a short, honest list — and from that list, one task stands out clearly as the place to start.

Why the first choice matters more than the tool

It is tempting to begin with the tool. Which model, which subscription, local or cloud? Those questions feel productive, but they are almost never the reason an AI project stalls. The real question is much simpler: which task is worth automating first?

A task is a good first candidate when it passes three tests:

  • It repeats. It comes back every day, week or month, so a routine you set up once keeps paying off.
  • It is low-risk. A draft that still needs your review is fine; a decision that must be right the first time is not a first task.
  • It drains you. It is the task you postpone, the one you quietly resent doing by hand.

The one-week audit, in four quiet steps

You don't need a complicated time-tracking system. A small notebook, a notes app or a simple spreadsheet is enough.

Step 1 — Note the tasks, not the minutes

For five working days, write down every administrative task as it lands: answering routine emails, writing offers, chasing invoices, updating client files, preparing meeting notes. Don't measure minutes — just list what you did and whether you would rather hand it to someone else.

Step 2 — Mark the repeaters

At the end of the week, mark every task that came up more than once. These are your repeaters. A task that appeared five times in one week is worth far more than a rare one-off, even if the one-off took longer.

Step 3 — Score each repeater

Give each repeating task a quick score from one to three for how much you dislike it, how often it returns, and how safe it would be to delegate a draft. Add the three numbers together. The highest total is your shortlist.

Step 4 — Pick one, and only one

Choose the single highest-scoring task and commit to automating just that one for the next month. Not three, not five — one. Starting small is how a new routine actually sticks.

A prompt to find the right one for you

If the list still feels unclear, hand the week's notes to the AI and let it help you rank them:

I am a [notary / fiduciary / doctor / small office] in Switzerland. Here is the list of administrative tasks I did last week and how often each came up: [list]. Help me rank them by (1) how repetitive they are, (2) how low-risk it is to produce a first draft, and (3) how much time they consume. Recommend the single best task to automate first, and explain your reasoning in two sentences.

What a good first task looks like in practice

In a notary's office it is often the intake summary or the first draft of a standard letter. In a fiduciary's practice it is the reminder email or the booking suggestion. For a doctor it is the dictation and the referral letter. In every case the pattern is the same: something that repeats, something a careful human always reviews, and something you will be glad never to type from scratch again.

One honest caveat

This audit is not a productivity contest. You are not measuring yourself against a standard, and the goal is not to squeeze more hours out of every day. You are simply noticing, calmly and honestly, where the friction sits — so that the first step you take is the right one.

The outcome

After one quiet week you have a short list of your real repeaters, a score that points to the right one, and a single, clearly chosen first AI task. You can start with confidence instead of the vague feeling that you should finally do something with AI — and the rest can wait, calmly, until you are ready.

Why reminders get postponed

Most self-employed people and small offices do not have a collections department. Reminders get written in a hurry between two jobs, or not at all. The usual reasons:

  • It feels personal: you like the client and do not want to strain the relationship.
  • It sits low on the list: the next client meeting always feels more important than an old invoice.
  • The wording is hard: too soft and it gets ignored, too hard and it gets awkward.

A three-step routine

Step 1 — One quiet list of open invoices

Once a week, gather the invoices that are past their due date — from your accounting tool, a spreadsheet, or a simple note. Keep it small and regular; five minutes is enough. The list only needs the client name, invoice number, amount, due date and days overdue.

Step 2 — The AI drafts, you decide the tone

Give the AI your list and a short description of how you want to sound: polite, firm, friendly but clear. The AI drafts a short reminder for each client, with the right facts already filled in. You read it, adjust a word if needed, and send.

Step 3 — Escalate gently, only when needed

If a first reminder brings no answer, the AI drafts the next step: a slightly firmer second reminder, and later a short note about the consequences of late payment — late fees and interest — always factual, never emotional.

The client below has not answered my first reminder from two weeks ago. Write a second, slightly firmer reminder. Stay polite and factual, refer to the previous reminder, and mention that I will have to pass the case to my fiduciary if it stays unpaid. No anger, no ultimatums.

  • Self-employed and independent professionals: a small stack of invoices, cleared in one weekly pass.
  • Fiduciaries: reminders sent on behalf of clients, always in the same clear, factual tone.
  • Doctors and small practices: billing that quietly follows up instead of stalling.
  • Notaries and law firms: fee notes that get a polite nudge instead of a long silence.

The routine is the same everywhere; only the wording changes.

The tone matters as much as the words. A good reminder is warm and clear: thank the client for the work together, state the facts, and ask for a date. It never threatens and never apologises for asking. On data, keep the same rule as everywhere else: do not paste confidential details into a public chatbot. Invoice numbers and amounts are usually fine, but for sensitive clients, anonymise first and add the real names back at the end.

The outcome

One half-hour a week is usually enough to keep cash flow healthy. The reminders go out on time, the awkwardness disappears, and most clients simply pay — because a polite, clear reminder is often all it takes. You stop carrying the unpaid invoices around in your head, and you get back to the work you are actually paid for.

The screen feels familiar: a ribbon at the top, a formula bar, the usual keyboard shortcuts, Paste Special. A spreadsheet an AI can operate directly

The feature the reviewers flagged first is the “agent-native” design. Every ribbon button, menu entry and keystroke in GridCraft also exists as a command that an AI assistant can call — through a standard interface (an “MCP server”, the emerging plug that connects AI assistants to everyday programs) or through the command line.

In everyday terms: instead of an AI guessing what it sees on a screenshot, it gets real hands. You could ask it to “tidy the client column, build a pivot table per canton, and add a chart” — and the program performs those clicks itself. For most Swiss self-employed people and small firms the sensible reading is: this is a direction, not a must-install. Two shifts are worth noticing. Office software is becoming local and private again — files that never leave your own machine sit comfortably with the revised Swiss data protection law. And programs are learning to be driven by AI directly, not only by mouse.

  1. If you can build it, or hire an hour of help: start with a copy of a workbook, never with the original.
  2. Open the copy in GridCraft, save it, reopen it in Excel — and compare formulas, formatting and charts.
  3. Give the assistant small, checkable jobs first: sort a column, clean duplicates, build a pivot table. Confirm every result.
  4. Keep Excel or your fiduciary software for everything that goes to the tax office.

Treat GridCraft as a preview of the next office normal: one program that speaks both human — a familiar ribbon — and machine, through a complete command set, on your own computer, for free. The tools your office runs on are learning to be operated. Make sure the operating instructions stay in your hands.

  • The re-entry looks scary: the inbox, the missed calls and the open pendences all pile up while you are away.
  • There is no one to hand over to: the business runs on your head, so leaving feels impossible.
  • The out-of-office is hard to write: a good one does more than say "I am away" — and that takes time you do not have before departure.

The result is predictable: you never really switch off, the holiday is half-work anyway, and you come back more tired than you left.

A three-step routine

Step 1 — Write the out-of-office before you leave

A week before departure, give the AI your travel dates, your usual tone and one or two contact people. It drafts an out-of-office reply that is warm, clear and genuinely useful — it states when you are back, who can help in the meantime, and what a client should do if it is urgent.

I am away from 24 to 31 August. Write a short out-of-office reply in my usual tone. State the dates, point clients to my colleague Anna for urgent matters, and add one friendly sentence telling them I will answer everything else when I am back. No drama, just a clear, warm note.

Step 2 — A quiet handover for the few things that cannot wait

Before you leave, make a short list of what is open. The AI turns it into a tidy handover note: what each item is about, where it stands, and what the next step is. You send it to your stand-in, a colleague or your fiduciary — and you genuinely let go.

Here are my open pendences for the week I am away. Sort them into two groups: things that can wait until I am back, and things someone must handle now. For each urgent item, write one line on what it is about and what the next step is.

Step 3 — Re-enter without the pile-up

On the day you return, the AI summarises what happened while you were away: the new emails, the answered ones, and anything that still needs you. You start with a tidy list instead of a wall of unread messages.

Summarise my inbox from the last week. List the new clients, the questions that were already answered, and the few things that still need my attention. Keep it to one page.

Why this works in practice

  • It removes the fear of leaving: the out-of-office and the handover already exist, so there is nothing left to dread.
  • It makes the re-entry: you come back to a summary, not a pile.
  • It protects the relationship: clients get a warm, clear answer even while you are away.

What this looks like across professions

  • Self-employed and independent professionals: a proper out-of-office and a quiet handover, so the holiday actually happens.
  • Fiduciaries: a clear note for clients about who handles what during the absence, always in the same tone.
  • Doctors and small practices: a locum handover that covers the open patients and the pending results.
  • Notaries and small offices: a tidy list of what is open, so the stand-in steps in without guesswork.

The routine is the same everywhere; only the wording changes.

A note on tone and data

The tone matters as much as the words. A good out-of-office is warm and short: state the dates, name the person who helps, and keep the promise to answer the rest on return. On data, keep the same rule as everywhere else: no confidential details in a public chatbot. Client names and file numbers stay out of the prompt; anonymise first and add the real names back into the final note yourself.

The outcome

One quiet hour before departure is usually enough to prepare a real holiday. The out-of-office is written, the handover is clear, and the re-entry is a single page instead of a pile. You switch off, come back rested, and the clients never noticed you were gone — because a prepared absence looks a lot like a well-run business.

You do not need to scan, file and answer everything yourself. Three quiet steps, done once a day, are enough.

Step 1 — Photograph the stack

Ten quiet minutes in the morning are usually enough to turn a mixed stack of paper into a short, sorted list. Nothing important slips through, the invoices reach bookkeeping on time, and the pile on the corner of the desk stops growing. The mail still arrives every day — but it stops running your morning.

Writing the Swiss Job Reference: An AI Routine for Employers

HR Legal Documents

Under Swiss law, an employee who asks for a reference is entitled to one that is truthful, benevolent and complete (Art. 330a of the Code of Obligations). That sounds simple. In practice it is a short, delicate piece of writing that many employers dread — and rush through at the last minute.

In a notary's office, a fiduciary, a doctor's practice or any small Swiss firm, a job reference is written only now and then, often for someone you have worked alongside for years. The stakes feel high, the phrasing is famously coded, and it always seems to land on your desk at the worst possible moment.

Why references feel heavier than they look

A job reference is only a page long, yet it carries a surprising amount of weight:

  • The law sets the frame. A reference must be true, well-meaning and complete — omitting an important fact can be just as problematic as getting one wrong.
  • The phrasing is coded. «to our full satisfaction» and «he made every effort» mean two very different things to a future employer who knows how to read between the lines.
  • It is personal. You are writing about a real colleague, and those words follow them to their next job.

What AI can do — and what only you can do

AI is well suited to the mechanical part: the structure, the standard sentences, keeping the tone even and benevolent, and switching between German, French and English. It can turn a handful of facts into a clean first draft in a few minutes.

What AI cannot do is decide the grades. You know whether someone exceeded expectations or simply met them; no model can know that for you. The AI drafts, you judge. That division of labour is the whole trick.

A simple routine to write one

Step 1 — Gather the facts

Write down the essentials in plain bullets: the person's name, their role, the start and end date, the main responsibilities, and two or three concrete achievements. This short list is all the AI needs.

Step 2 — Decide the grades

Go through the usual categories — quality of work, quantity, initiative, conduct with clients and colleagues — and mark each one honestly: above expectations, fully met, or met. Do this before you open the AI, so the draft reflects your judgement rather than the model's guesses.

Step 3 — Let the AI draft

Give the AI your facts and grades and ask for a Swiss reference in the classic style:

I am a Swiss employer. Please write a job reference (Arbeitszeugnis) for [name], who worked as [role] from [start] to [end]. Main tasks: [list them]. Grades on the Swiss scale: quality of work — [above expectations / fully met / met], conduct with clients and colleagues — [above expectations / fully met / met], initiative — [above expectations / fully met / met]. Write it in the conventional Swiss style: warm but truthful and complete, using the standard phrasing for each grade. Keep it to one page.

Step 4 — Read it aloud

Print the draft and read it once, sentence by sentence, against your honest opinion. If a sentence feels a notch too generous or a touch too cool, adjust it. The final word is always yours.

The phrases that carry the grade

A Swiss reference speaks in a quiet code. A future employer reads these phrases as a scale, so it is worth knowing what you are signing:

  • «always to our fullest satisfaction» — excellent
  • «to our full satisfaction» — good
  • «to our satisfaction» — satisfactory
  • «he/she made an effort» — below expectations, a gentle warning

A useful rule of thumb: the warmer and more specific the wording, the better the hidden grade. If a reference praises punctuality at length and says little about the work itself, a careful reader notices.

A second prompt for the multilingual version

Swiss teams are often multilingual, and a reference written once may need to exist in German, French and English. Ask the AI to produce all three from the same facts, keeping the coded grades consistent:

Translate this job reference into French and English, keeping the Swiss reference conventions and making sure the grade implied by each phrase stays consistent across all three versions.

The outcome

A task that once cost a stressed evening and a vague «did I phrase that right?» becomes one sitting: gather the facts, set the grades, let the AI draft, and sign a reference you can stand behind. The person leaving gets a fair, warm send-off — and you get the certainty that every sentence is deliberate.

\n\n

Kev answers yes/no, multiple-choice, or rating questions about a piece of text and returns calibrated probabilities in one pass. It is built for ticket routing, moderation, and classification — not free-text generation. Think of it as a wire-compatible drop-in replacement for paid services like Jev (the closed model behind TypeSafe's System One API), except you host it yourself or run the 4B model locally on a machine you own.

\n\n

Three tasks that usually pay off first

\n\n

In our work with Swiss freelancers, notaries, doctors and small offices, three classification tasks almost always repay the effort:

  • Ticket routing. Incoming client emails or support requests can be automatically directed to the right team or flagged for follow-up based on content keywords.

  • Document categorisation. Contracts, letters and quotes can be classified by type, urgency or required action — without sending client data to a cloud API.

Start with exactly one of these. One task, one channel, one clear win.

\n\n

Which model size do you actually need?

Kev ships four sizes together as "Kev 1.0": 0.8B, 4B (the recommended default), 9B, and 27B. Under the Swiss Data Protection Act (DSG), do not feed identifiable client information — names, medical notes, financial details — into a public consumer tool without checking. The practical fix is simple: anonymise or replace identifying details first, and for sensitive work in medicine, law or finance, use an approved or local setup. That is the honest version of “getting started.” No transformation, no agents, no hype — just one repetitive classification task that no longer eats your afternoon.

Use case 1: Answering common customer questions

An agent can answer the questions that repeat every week — opening hours, how your process works, what a job roughly costs, how long a turnaround takes. The crucial detail: it answers from a written FAQ you maintain, not from its general knowledge. When the answer is documented, the agent drafts a reply in your tone and you approve it. When it is not documented, the agent does not know that — it produces a confident answer anyway, and the confident answer may be wrong. So the agent only works here if you have already written the answers down, or are willing to spend an afternoon doing so.

Use case 2: Drafting quotes

Here the agent is a writing assistant, not a pricing engine. Given your price list, a past quote as an example and the client’s inquiry, it assembles a first draft — structure, wording, the polite parts — in minutes. What it must never do is invent the numbers. Prices, discounts and delivery times come from your systems and your judgment; the agent arranges them into prose. Set that rule explicitly, check every figure before sending, and drafting time drops noticeably. Skip the rule, and one wrong price in one sent quote costs more than every saved minute.

Use case 3: Following up on leads

The unglamorous winner. Most small businesses lose work not because clients say no, but because nobody follows up. An agent that watches unanswered inquiries and drafts a short, friendly nudge after three days — and again after ten — is genuinely useful, because the task is formulaic and the failure mode is silence. The guardrail: you approve each message before it goes. An agent that follows up on its own eventually messages the client who asked you to call back in January — in November.

Where agents create more work than they save

  • Undocumented processes: if the knowledge lives only in your head, you end up writing instructions for the agent — and answering its questions all week.
  • Low volume: ten inquiries a month do not justify a setup plus supervision. A template and a calendar reminder do the same job.
  • Costly errors: a wrong answer sent to a client is your mistake, not the agent’s. The higher the stakes, the more the human check eats the savings.
  • No owner: if nobody reviews the output, nobody trusts it — and the work happens twice.

A three-question test

  1. Is the task repetitive, with rules you could write down in an afternoon?
  2. Would a thirty-second human check catch a bad output before it reaches a client?
  3. Can you spare fifteen minutes a week to supervise it?

Three times yes: pick one use case, run a four-week pilot with you in the loop, and measure the hours saved. Any no: fix the underlying process first — write the FAQ, standardise the quote, set the reminder. Often that alone removes the need for an agent; and if you later add one, it will have something solid to stand on.

“An agent is a tireless junior assistant with zero accountability. Treat it like one: give written instructions, check the work, and never let it sign anything.”

Why careful offers still get turned down

When a client goes quiet after receiving an offer, it is usually for one of four reasons:

  • Fuzzy scope: the client cannot tell what is included — and what would cost extra.
  • An unexplained price: a total without a breakdown reads as arbitrary, even when it is fair.
  • Unanswered questions: the offer answers the request you remembered, not the one the client actually wrote.

  • Restating the request. Paste the client’s email or chat messages and have the AI summarise what they asked for, in their own words. An offer that visibly answers the client’s actual request starts ahead of most competitors.
  • Keeping the structure consistent. A fixed skeleton — task, approach, deliverables, price, next step, validity date — means nothing important gets forgotten when you are tired.

Keep three things firmly human. First, pricing: a model knows nothing about your margins, your capacity or the going rates in your region.   3. Draft with your own material. Give the AI your structure, an anonymised past offer and the confirmed facts. Use placeholders for prices and deadlines.
  4. Check the substance. Every deliverable priced, nothing promised that you cannot deliver, every figure from your notes — not from the model.
  5. Make it personal. Add the one detail that shows why you are the right fit, and close with a concrete next step and a date.
“Draft this offer from the client’s request below and my example offer. Use placeholders for prices and deadlines. Do not add deliverables I have not listed. Flag anything the request leaves unclear.”

What to measure

Track three numbers: offers sent per month, reply rate, and time spent per offer. If a 30-minute offer replaces a two-hour one, you will send more of them — and following up stops feeling like a chore. That is usually where the real gains appear, long before any wording magic.

And when an offer is accepted, the next step should be just as clean: send a proper Swiss invoice with a QR-bill, correct payment terms and clean numbering, so the momentum is not lost in admin.

Avoiding AI Vendor Lock-in: Keeping Your Business Data Portable

StrategyData protectionCosts

The monthly subscription is the visible cost of an AI assistant. The invisible cost is how hard it becomes to leave. A year in, your chat history, your uploaded documents, your custom instructions and your team’s working habits all live inside one provider’s platform. For a Swiss SME or a self-employed professional, that quiet accumulation deserves a plan — not paranoia, just a handful of habits that keep the exit door open.

Where your data actually ends up

Modern AI tools are convenient precisely because they remember. The conversation history holds the context of your business: how you phrase offers, which tone you use with which client, what you decided last month. Uploaded files — drafts, contracts, meeting notes — often stay attached to those chats. Custom instructions, prompt libraries and configured assistants or agents live in the tool’s settings. Team plans add shared projects and knowledge bases. None of this is malicious; the product works exactly as designed. But it means the tool slowly becomes the only place where your way of working is written down.

What you can realistically export

The major providers do offer a data export, usually buried in the account settings. You typically receive a ZIP archive with your conversations and uploaded files, in JSON or HTML form. That is enough to read and to keep, but not enough to move: the formats are not standardised, and a conversation from one assistant does not slot neatly into another. Exports are also snapshots — whatever was discussed since your last download stays behind. And plenty of smaller tools offer no export at all.

Five habits that keep you free to switch

  • Keep the masters on your own machine. The AI works on copies; the authoritative version of an offer, a letter or a process document lives in your own folder structure — and in your own backup, not inside a chat.
  • Maintain a prompt library outside the tool. Your best prompts, custom instructions and style notes belong in a document you own. If they exist only on a settings page, a switch means rebuilding them from memory.
  • Schedule a quarterly export. A recurring thirty-minute calendar entry: download the export, store it with your backups. Boring — and exactly the point.
  • Save output in open formats. Markdown or plain text beats a proprietary project file you may not be able to open elsewhere.
  • Check the exit before you buy. Before adopting a new AI tool, find the export function first. If there is none, decide consciously whether what you put in is something you can afford to leave behind.

The Swiss legal footnote

One honest caveat: the revised Swiss Data Protection Act, in force since September 2023, strengthens your information rights — but unlike the EU’s GDPR, it contains no explicit right to data portability. The law will not move your data for you. And for client data you process, you remain responsible no matter which tool holds it. Portability is a practical task, settled in contracts and habits rather than in court.

The one-evening exit test

Once a year, ask a simple question: if the subscription doubled tomorrow, or the terms changed in a way you cannot accept, could you move to another tool in a single evening? The chat history matters less than you think; the slow part is re-teaching the context — prompts, instructions, templates, habits. If all of that is stored on your side, the exit stays cheap. If it lives only in the tool, you do not own the workflow; the provider does.

“Convenience is what you buy. Portability is what you keep. Set up the exit before you fall in love with the tool.”

AI for a One-Person Business: A 30-Day Starter Plan for Swiss Solo Self-Employed

A one-person business has no IT department, no budget for pilot projects and nobody to hand the experiment to. That is exactly why a structured start matters more for a Swiss solo self-employed person than for a company with fifty staff: you cannot afford evenings spent on tools that lead nowhere. This 30-day plan moves in weeks, not in one heroic sprint — and every step is tested against your real work, not against a demo.

Why 30 days and not one weekend

Most solo businesses fail with AI for a predictable reason: they try everything in a single evening, get mediocre output, and conclude the technology is overhyped. A month gives you the one thing a weekend cannot — repetition. A workflow only counts if it survives four weeks of real client emails, real invoices and real deadlines.

On cost: start with one paid subscription to a mainstream assistant (typically around CHF 20–30 per month) and nothing else. Ignore every other tool until day 30. The plan is deliberately tool-agnostic; the value is in the routine, not in the brand.

Week 1 (days 1–7): choose one task

Do not start with a tool — start with your time. List every task from last week that took longer than 15 minutes and recurs at least twice a week. For most Swiss one-person businesses the shortlist looks the same: answering routine client emails, writing offers, chasing open invoices, turning meeting notes into next steps.

Pick exactly one. Set up your assistant and do that single task with it every day this week. Nothing else. The goal is to learn what the tool does well on your work, not to build a showcase.

Week 2 (days 8–14): make it sound like you

Writing tasks are where most one-person businesses see the first real gains, because you already know what a good result looks like. Build one reusable prompt template with four parts: who you are and what you offer, the specific task, the tone, and a short sample of text you wrote yourself. The sample does more than any adjective — it is what stops the output from sounding like a machine.

Two rules keep this safe. First: the AI drafts, you decide — never send what you have not read. Second: under the Swiss Data Protection Act (nDSG) you remain responsible for client data, so check where a tool processes and stores data before you paste a client file into it.

Week 3 (days 15–21): add one admin workflow

Now add a second, administrative workflow with a clearly verifiable result: payment reminders, checking invoice details before they go out, or summarising a long document into bullet points. Admin tasks are lower-risk than writing, because errors are visible immediately — a wrong figure in a reminder catches your eye long before the client ever sees it.

Keep a simple list of what you handed over, and note every time the output needed a correction. That list becomes your evidence in week 4.

Week 4 (days 22–30): measure, keep, cut

Honest accounting beats enthusiasm. How much time did the two workflows actually save? Which results needed so much correction that they cost time instead of freeing it? Cut what did not work — that discipline is worth more than any new subscription. Save the prompts that worked into a single file; they are business assets you will reuse for years. Then choose the one workflow you will add next month. Not five.

What this plan will not do

It will not run your business. AI drafts, summarises and checks — you verify, sign and carry the responsibility, contractually and under data protection law. It will also not rescue a messy process: if your invoicing lives in chaos, a language model just produces the chaos faster. Fix the process first, then automate it.

Thirty days, two workflows, one subscription. That is a realistic start — and in a one-person business, realistic is what survives.

Künstliche Intelligenz ist für Schweizer KMUs und Selbstständige kein ferner Zukunftstrend — sie ist ein Werkzeug, das jetzt bereits administrative Lasten abnehmen, Entscheidungen beschleunigen und Zeit für das Wesentliche freisetzen kann. Wo KI jetzt schon hilft

Es gibt Bereiche, in denen KI schnell spürbare Entlastung schafft:

  • Dokumentenzusammenfassungen: Lange Angebote, Verträge oder Kreisbriefe lassen sich in kurze Punkte herunterbrechen, ohne dass der Inhalt verloren geht.
  • E-Mail‑ und Antwortentwürfe: Ein kurzer Prompt genügt, um professionelle Antworten in Ihrem Ton zu erhalten, die nur noch einer kleinen Überprüfung bedürfen.
  • Terminplanung und Erinnerungen: KI kann Anfragen nach Terminen extrahieren, passende Zeitfenster vorschlagen und Erinnerungen erstellen, damit nichts durch die Lücke geht.

Der schrittweise Einstieg

Beginnen Sie nicht mit einer firmweiten KI-Strategie, sondern mit einem einzigen, wiederkehrenden Aufgabenbereich:

  1. Wählen Sie eine Routine aus, die Sie wöchentlich wiederholen (z. B. Angebots-Erstellung, Rechnungserinnerungen oder Kunden‑Follow‑ups).
  2. Prüfen Sie, welche Daten dafür benötigt werden und ob diese lokal oder in einem geschützten Bereich liegen.
  3. Testen Sie ein einfaches KI-Tool mit diesen Daten — starten Sie mit einer Testgruppe oder anonymisierten Beispielunterlagen.

  5. Entscheiden Sie, ob Sie den Einsatz ausbauen oder bei diesem Beispiel bleiben.

So entwickeln Sie nach und nach ein Gefühl dafür, wo KI echten Mehrwert stiftet und wo traditionelle Methoden besser aufgehoben sind.

Wichtige Rahmenbedingungen

Wenn Sie mit KI arbeiten, sollten diese Grundregeln gelten:

  • Keine sensibenten Kundendaten in öffentliche Consumer-Tools eingeben, es sei denn, Sie haben geprüft, dass die Daten dort sicher aufgehoben sind.
  • Identifizierende Informationen entfernen oder durch Platzhalter ersetzen, wenn Sie Tools testen.
  • Das finale Ergebnis immer menschlich prüfen, bevor es an Kunden oder Partner geht.
  • Klare interne Regeln festlegen, welche Aufgaben KI übernehmen darf und welche nicht.

Das Ziel ist einfach: weniger administrative Last, mehr Zeit für die Kernarbeit — und ein Praxis-Check, ob die verwendete Lösung auch wirklich zu Ihrem Unternehmen passt.

Where AI Still Fails: An Honest Guide for Swiss SMEs

AI BasicsQualityStrategy

AI demos are impressive. Then you run the same tool on your own invoices, contracts or client emails — and it quietly gets something wrong. These failures are not random. They are predictable, and knowing them is the difference between a useful assistant and an expensive source of mistakes.

The failures you will actually run into

Numbers. Ask an AI to total a long expense table, split an invoice or check a VAT rate, and it can hand you a confident, wrong figure. Language models produce plausible arithmetic, not verified arithmetic. Anything that touches money stays a draft until a human or a spreadsheet confirms it.

Sources. Models sometimes invent citations: a court ruling, an article number of the Code of Obligations, a study that does not exist. The sentence looks perfect; the reference is fiction. If a claim matters — legally, financially, medically — open the source yourself before you repeat it.

Context. Every model has a hard limit on how much text it genuinely holds in mind. A 120-page contract, a year of correspondence, a full payroll file: the AI may read the opening well and miss the clause on page 40. Splitting a document into chunks helps, but cross-references between the chunks get lost. Long documents need targeted questions, not “summarise everything”.

Chains of steps. An AI agent that plans and executes drifts: it takes a wrong turn early and keeps going confidently. That is tolerable for research; it is not tolerable for booking payments or sending mail on its own. Every chain of AI steps needs a human checkpoint before anything leaves the building.

Responsibility. AI cannot sign anything, cannot be held liable, and cannot exercise professional discretion. It can draft the letter; you decide whether it is sent. This is not a limit that next year’s model will fix — it is the nature of the tool.

Where AI is genuinely reliable today

Drafting and restructuring text. Summarising documents you already know. Translating between German, French and English. Turning messy notes into a clean structure, or a technical explanation into something a client actually understands. Here AI saves real hours and rarely embarrasses you — because you review the result anyway, and the mistakes are easy to catch.

“AI does not fail at random. It fails in predictable places: numbers, sources, long documents, chains of steps and anything that carries responsibility. Put a human between the AI and those five things, and the rest is leverage.”

A simple trust test before you hand off a task

  1. Take five real cases where you already know the correct answer.
  2. Run the AI on them exactly as you would in daily work.
  3. Count the errors — and estimate how long each one would take to catch.
  4. Hand off the task only if checking the output is faster than doing the work yourself.

Keep a short list of the tasks where AI failed, and why. Models improve quickly, and a limit that held in spring may be gone by winter — but it disappears for the people who retest, not for the people who gave up.

What this means for your business

Use AI where it is strong: drafting, summarising, translating, structuring. Keep a human on the five weak spots — or at least a verification step in between. That is the whole strategy, and it is an honest one: not “AI can do everything”, and not “AI is useless”, but “AI is strong exactly here, and weak exactly there”.

Client Letters That Still Sound Like You: A Practical AI Workflow

Client CommunicationVoice & ToneWorkflow

A client letter can be correct and still feel unlike you. AI makes it easy to produce a polished first draft, but generic warmth, inflated promises or an unfamiliar formality can undermine a relationship you have built over years. For a Swiss freelancer or small firm, the useful goal is not to let a model impersonate you. It is to make routine writing quicker while keeping your judgement, facts and voice in charge.

This is a different problem from translation. Whether you write in German, French, Italian or English, the client should still recognise the same business behind the words. Start by teaching the tool how you communicate, then keep a human review before anything is sent.

Why AI drafts can sound generic

A model has no reliable access to your personality. If you ask it to “write a friendly reply”, it reaches for familiar phrases: “I hope this email finds you well”, “delighted to assist”, or a level of enthusiasm you would never use. The result may be grammatically smooth but wrong for a small Swiss practice where clients value clarity, restraint and dependable follow-through.

It can also change the meaning while improving the rhythm. A tentative estimate can become a firm commitment; a request for documents can turn into an implied approval. Voice is not just adjectives. It includes what you promise, how directly you speak and where you draw a boundary.

Make a one-page voice guide

Do not begin with a long prompt or a marketing persona. Collect three to five short messages you wrote yourself: perhaps an appointment confirmation, a response to a common question and a polite refusal. Remove names, contact details, case information and anything confidential. Then describe the patterns you want the assistant to follow:

  • Formality: Do you use “Sie” or “du”? How do you greet a familiar client versus a new contact?
  • Length: Do you prefer a direct answer in one paragraph, or a short explanation with bullets?
  • Tone: Are you warm and conversational, or precise and reserved? List words you would and would not use.
  • Boundaries: Never invent facts, deadlines, prices or commitments; mark missing information with a question.

Use examples as guidance, not as a template to copy blindly. A model can imitate surface features, but only you can decide what feels authentic.

A review-first drafting workflow

  1. Give it the context. Provide the client’s question, the verified facts and the action you want to propose. Use placeholders for names and sensitive details unless your approved tool and settings permit the real data.
  2. Attach the voice guide. Ask for a concise draft in your usual style. Tell the model to preserve the meaning, avoid adding facts and flag anything it cannot answer from the information supplied.
  3. Check the substance first. Compare every date, amount, name and commitment against your source. Remove any promise you have not authorised. Only then edit for voice.
  4. Make the final personal adjustment. Replace stock phrases, add the specific detail that shows you understood the client, and read the message aloud. If you would not say it on a call, rewrite it.
“Use my examples to match my usual level of formality and brevity. Do not invent information or commitments. If a fact is missing, ask me instead of guessing. Draft only; do not send.”

What to measure—and what to keep human

Try the workflow on one recurring, low-risk message for two weeks. Count the minutes saved after checking and editing, not the time spent generating a draft. Note how often you correct tone, facts or an unintended promise. If review takes as long as writing from scratch, improve the examples or stop using AI for that message.

Keep sensitive matters, complaints, negotiations and professional advice under direct human control. Swiss data-protection and confidentiality duties still apply: minimise personal information, check the provider’s terms and retention settings, and do not paste client records into an unapproved consumer account. AI can help you get to a good draft sooner; the relationship, responsibility and send button remain yours.

Turning Meeting Notes Into Action Items: An AI Routine for Swiss Self-Employed

The client call ends well. You scribble three lines — “send offer, clarify VAT, ask about the March deadline” — and get back to work. Ten days later the note resurfaces under an invoice, the deadline has passed, and the client politely asks whether you are still interested. The meeting was never the problem. The step from notes to action is — and that is exactly the step AI handles well, if you build it as a routine rather than a party trick.

Notes capture moments, not commitments

A note says “VAT question”. A task says “call Mr Brunner by Thursday and confirm the VAT rate for the March offer”. Notes are compressed memory for the person who was in the room; tasks are commitments that survive a busy week. In a larger company, a project manager converts one into the other. When you are self-employed, nobody does — and that is where client work quietly dies. Not laziness: a missing step in the workflow.

The routine: ten minutes, three steps

  1. Dump everything, unfiltered. Right after the conversation — or as a twice-weekly pass — collect what actually exists: the scribbled page, the voice memo from the walk back to the office, the photo of the whiteboard, the half-sentence in a chat. Do not tidy up first; tidying is the machine’s job.
  2. One structured prompt. Ask for three separate lists: action items (task, owner, deadline if one was genuinely agreed), decisions made, and open questions. The crucial instruction: wherever the notes are vague, the AI must write “unclear” — not guess.
  3. Verify, then move. Walk the list once against your own memory of the conversation. Then put the tasks where tasks belong — your to-do list or calendar, not the chat window nobody reopens on Thursday morning.

Where AI genuinely helps — and where it invents

The strengths are real. It is relentlessly structured, it catches items you forgot you even wrote down, it never tires of formatting, and it drafts the two-line recap to the client (“Here is what we agreed; the offer follows by Friday”) that makes a one-person business look organised.

The weakness is just as real: language models fill gaps. If your note says “clarify VAT”, the model cheerfully writes “clarify VAT by Friday” — a deadline nobody agreed to. An action item with an invented date is worse than no action item, because you now trust it. Two rules keep the output honest: every deadline is confirmed against the source, and anything marked “unclear” goes back to the client as a question — not into your task list as a guess.

Client data stays out of the prompt

Meeting notes are among the most sensitive documents a self-employed person holds: names, figures, deadlines, sometimes health or legal details. The revised Swiss Data Protection Act (nDSG) does not forbid AI here — it obliges you to choose tools and providers deliberately. In practice: replace names with “Client A” and amounts with placeholders before pasting into a cloud tool, or run a local model that never leaves your computer. Turning notes into tasks does not need real names; “Client A, offer by Friday” works just as well.

“Here are my raw notes from a client meeting. Produce three lists: (1) action items — task, owner, deadline, only where a date was explicitly agreed; (2) decisions made; (3) open questions. Write ‘unclear’ wherever the notes are vague. Do not invent dates, names or amounts. Keep it short and factual.”

The habit that makes it work

Run the pass within a few hours of the meeting, while your memory can still check the output — a week later it is archaeology, not administration. Done this way, the offer goes out on Friday as promised, the VAT question is answered before the client asks again, and the “what exactly did we agree?” evening disappears from your week. That is the entire point: not beautiful minutes, but kept promises.

GPT, Claude or Local? Choosing an AI Model for Your Swiss Business

Every few weeks a new AI model tops a leaderboard, and every few weeks a client asks us the same question: which one should our business actually use? The honest answer for a Swiss SME is that for most office work the choice matters less than the marketing suggests. But it does matter — in three specific situations. Here is a calm way to decide between GPT, Claude and a local model, without re-running the comparison every month.

What actually differs between models

For everyday office work — drafting a client letter, summarising a ten-page contract, answering routine email — the leading models are close enough that you will rarely notice a difference. The gaps appear in specific corners: very long documents, complex tables, unusual formatting, and questions where the model should admit it does not know. Claude has a reputation for careful work on long documents, GPT for breadth and integrations, and local models sit a step behind on peak quality but handle routine text reliably.

One warning: any concrete ranking you read — including this one — is outdated within a few months. Treat model names as interchangeable candidates, not as long-term commitments.

Test with your language, not with English benchmarks

Benchmarks run in English. Your clients write in German and French, with Swiss conventions: formal salutations, amounts in CHF, and “Sie” and “vous” used correctly. Before you commit, run ten of your real tasks through a candidate model — an actual offer, a real reply to a complaint, a genuine French letter. Most top models handle both languages well today, but formality levels and formatting conventions are still where they trip. The model that wins an English benchmark is not automatically the model that writes your letters well.

When local is the right answer

If your work involves data you are not allowed to send to a cloud provider — patient files, legal cases, client financials protected by professional secrecy and the nDSG — a local model on your own machine removes the question entirely: nothing leaves the building. The trade-off is real: lower peak quality, some setup effort, and hardware that has to be paid for. If your documents are routine letters and summaries, a good local model is enough. If you need the strongest analysis, use a cloud model on anonymised text and keep the sensitive original local.

A three-question rule

  1. How sensitive is the data? If it must not leave your machine, go local — or anonymise before using a cloud model.
  2. How demanding is the task? Routine text: any current model will do. Complex analysis or delicate formatting: use the strongest model you can access.
  3. What does it cost? For a one-to-five-person business, a flat-rate subscription of roughly CHF 20–30 per seat per month is almost always cheaper than paying per request. Start there, and upgrade only when you hit a wall.

Do not marry a model

Whichever you choose, keep the exit cheap. Store your prompts in a document, not only inside one chat app. Describe your workflows in plain language so that any model can run them. Then re-test every quarter with the same ten real tasks: models improve, prices change, and yesterday’s clear winner may sit in the middle of the pack tomorrow. Switching should take thirty minutes, not a migration project.

The model is the least stable part of your AI setup. Your workflows, your document structure and your routines are the durable parts. Build those so they run on whatever model is best next quarter — and stop worrying about the leaderboard.

  • Your clients notice. A fiduciary whose posts sound like a motivational calendar is contradicting the very precision clients pay for.
  • Consistency builds trust. Your voice should be recognisable across your website, your offers and your posts. If a post sounds like a different company, something quietly breaks.
  • Feeds reward real posts. Few platforms show bland, visibly generated content to many people — and those who do see it rarely act on it.

What AI is genuinely good at

  • Turning real work into ideas. After a project, one line in your notes is enough for the AI to suggest three post angles — without ever naming the client.
  • Drafting from your own material. Give the AI two or three of your past posts or newsletters as voice samples, and it drafts in your style instead of the average internet style.
  • Keeping the calendar alive. Planning a month of posts, adapting one piece for LinkedIn and Instagram, repurposing an old newsletter — mechanical work that AI handles well.

What AI cannot supply

Three things stay human. First, your opinions: a language model averages millions of voices — your actual take on a topic is the content. Second, your cases: never paste client names, figures or documents into a consumer AI tool; anonymise first, and check what the tool does with data under the revised Swiss Data Protection Act. Third, the moment itself: a photo from the actual site, the team or the workshop beats any generated image.

A practical weekly routine

  1. Keep a running note. After real work, write one line: the topic and what surprised you. No client names.
  2. Batch once a week. Give the AI your notes plus two or three of your best past posts as voice samples.
  3. Draft in a fixed structure. One hook, one concrete example, one useful takeaway, a plain next step.
  4. Edit like a human. Read it aloud, delete the buzzwords, check every fact — then cut ten per cent.
  5. Schedule and stop. Two good posts a month, published reliably, beat twenty rushed ones.
“Write a LinkedIn post from my note below, in the voice of my example posts. One concrete example, one takeaway, no emoji lists, no buzzwords, at most 120 words. Ask me if a fact is missing.”

What to measure

Do not count likes. Track the enquiries that mention your content, profile visits and direct messages — over months, not weeks. For most Swiss SMEs the audience is small but exactly right: a handful of potential clients reading carefully is worth more than a thousand anonymous impressions.

The goal is not to sound impressive. It is to sound like the person your clients will actually work with. AI gives you the consistency; you supply the character. That combination is exactly what generic posts never have.

AI for Your Swiss Tax Return: What It Helps With (and What It Can’t)

FinanceData protectionStrategy

Every spring, the same ritual: a folder of receipts, the canton’s forms, and the quiet hope that nothing is missing. AI can take a real chunk of work out of the Swiss tax return — sorting, explaining, checking. It cannot sign, file, or take responsibility. Here is the honest line between the two.

If you are self-employed in Switzerland, your business income lands in the same personal tax return as your salary and savings — plus supplementary forms for the self-employed. The return is due once a year, but the work piles up quietly all year round. AI helps most where that work is mechanical.

Where AI genuinely helps

  • Sorting the shoebox. Scan or photograph receipts and let AI pre-sort them into your bookkeeping categories — materials, software, travel, insurance — and flag anything that looks private. You confirm; it files.
  • Decoding the forms. Paste a paragraph from the return or a letter from the tax office and ask what it means for a self-employed person, in plain language. That alone removes most of the dread.
  • Checking completeness. Give the AI your list of attachments — income statement, balance sheet, receipts, open items — and ask what is missing before you submit.
  • Drafting explanation letters. When a position needs a note — an unusually high expense, a new vehicle, a one-off project — AI drafts the short letter in a calm, factual tone. You check the facts and sign.
  • Rough scenarios. “If my profit is around this figure, roughly what tax burden should I expect?” — useful for planning, never as a filing number.

Where AI stops

  1. It is not a tax advisor. A Swiss fiduciary answers for their work; a language model answers for nothing. Anything with legal consequences needs a human who carries liability.
  2. Cantons differ. Rates, deadlines and forms vary by canton and change every year, while models confidently reuse outdated or generic material. Verify against your canton’s current information.
  3. It does not calculate reliably. Models write well and add up poorly. Every figure in your return should come from your bookkeeping or a spreadsheet — never from a chat.
  4. It does not file. Submission still runs through your canton’s official software or your fiduciary. No AI tool files a Swiss tax return for you.

Your tax data deserves the most care

A finished return reveals your income, your clients, your family status and your account balances. The revised Federal Act on Data Protection (nDSG) obliges you to handle such data with care — that applies to AI tools too. Two working rules: strip names, social insurance numbers and amounts before pasting anything into a cloud tool — or use a local model that runs on your own computer. Explaining a tax concept does not need your real numbers.

“Explain what this field of the Swiss tax return means for a self-employed person, in plain language. Do not invent amounts or give legal advice; if you are unsure, say so.”

The useful habit starts now, not in March

The biggest AI contribution to your tax return is not a March marathon — it is a short monthly pass: receipts scanned and pre-sorted, open questions noted while they are fresh, explanations drafted while the facts are still in your head. In March you then assemble and check, instead of reconstructing and guessing.

A sensible division of labour

Use AI as the preparation layer: sorting, decoding, completeness checks, draft letters. Keep the decision layer human: the figures come from your accounts, the positions are yours, the final review is yours or your fiduciary’s — with a signature that carries weight. Set up this way, AI realistically saves you several evenings a year, without moving responsibility onto a tool that cannot carry it.

The Only AI Tools a Swiss SME Needs in 2026

ToolsCostsStrategy

Most Swiss SMEs don’t have an AI problem — they have a subscription problem. The marketing suggests a growing stack of specialised apps: one for writing, one for meetings, one for invoices, one for social posts. In practice, three well-chosen tools cover the large majority of what a small business actually does with AI in 2026. Everything else is optional until proven otherwise.

The core three

Watch what gets opened during a normal working week and the same three categories keep appearing:

  • One strong general assistant. ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini — one paid seat for each person who writes regularly. Drafting letters and offers, summarising documents, translating between German, French and English, making sense of a spreadsheet, preparing a meeting. This one seat delivers most of the measurable value, because it is the tool people actually use every day.
  • The AI already inside your office suite. If the company pays for Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace, Copilot or Gemini is either included or one add-on away. It drafts emails, recaps meetings and searches documents where those files already live. Test what your existing licence includes before buying anything new — many SMEs pay twice for the same capability.
  • A private option for sensitive data. A local model on the office laptop, or a cloud tool in a zero-retention configuration, for contracts, salary data and client files you would not paste into a random web form. This is the tool that keeps the other two out of trouble.

What you don’t need (yet)

Just as important is what to skip. You almost certainly don’t need a separate AI app for every task — the general assistant covers writing, summarising and translating. You don’t need an autonomous agent without one clearly defined weekly job. And you don’t need the “AI-powered” upgrade of software you barely used before it grew a chatbot. If a tool cannot name the recurring task it takes over, it is a gadget, not infrastructure.

Two rules before you subscribe

  1. The weekly-task test. A tool must take over a task you genuinely do every week — not a hypothetical one — and save more time than it costs. Price your own hour honestly: a CHF 30 subscription is cheap twice over if it removes two hours of admin, and expensive at zero if nobody opens it.
  2. The exit test. You must be able to export your data — prompts, documents, contact histories — in a format you can read without the vendor. Tools that hold your work hostage get more expensive every year, not less.

Then count the total. CHF 20 here, CHF 35 there, CHF 15 for something you forgot about: small subscriptions quietly become a four-figure annual budget. A stack is a cost centre until every line proves otherwise.

The Swiss specifics that matter

  • Data protection. Under the revised Swiss Data Protection Act, client data stays your responsibility no matter which tool processed it. Keep sensitive files with local or zero-retention options, and keep client names out of free web tools with unclear retention terms.
  • Language quality. Whatever you buy must write proper German and French, not just English. Test each tool with a real letter from your own archive before committing to an annual plan.
  • Data location. Many Swiss SMEs prefer hosting in Switzerland or the EU. It is not mandatory in every case, but it noticeably shortens client conversations.

An inventory, not a stack

Keep one page: every AI tool, its monthly cost, its renewal date, the recurring task it performs, and a rough estimate of hours saved. Review the page quarterly and cancel anything nobody has opened in three months. Three tools that are actually used beat fifteen that looked impressive in a demo — and a stack that is easy to explain is also the one that is easy to change when something better arrives in 2027.

The 10 Hours a Week AI Can Give Back to a Swiss Freelancer

ProductivityAutomationSmall business

“Save ten hours a week with AI” is one of the most repeated promises in tech marketing right now. In its usual form it is misleading: no single tool hands a freelancer ten free hours. But if you run a one-person business in Switzerland, ten reclaimed hours a week is a realistic aggregate — provided you know where those hours hide and what you intend to do with them.

Where the ten hours actually come from

Across the self-employed people we work with, the savings that add up to roughly ten hours a week come from unglamorous corners of the business, never from one spectacular automation:

  • Inbox triage and short replies (1–1.5 hours). Sorting the day’s mail, deciding what actually needs an answer, and drafting routine responses.
  • First drafts of offers and client letters (1.5–2 hours). The AI drafts from your notes and your own past wording; you edit instead of facing a blank page.
  • Meeting notes and follow-ups (1–1.5 hours). Turning a voice memo or a page of scribbles into minutes, decisions and next steps.
  • Admin: invoices, reminders, receipt chasing (1–1.5 hours). Drafting friendly payment reminders and collecting receipts is nobody’s favourite hour of the week.
  • Searching your own documents (about 1 hour). Finding the old offer, the contract clause or last year’s email thread without a twenty-minute hunt.
  • Staying in touch (about 1 hour). A short monthly newsletter, a LinkedIn post, a check-in message — drafted quickly, then genuinely personalised.
  • Weekly planning and review (about 1 hour). Summarising what happened, what is overdue, and what next week should focus on.

Add those up and you land somewhere between eight and eleven hours. That is where the marketing number comes from: it is the sum of many fifteen-minute savings, not a single windfall.

The catch: saved time only counts once you spend it deliberately

Here is the part the adverts skip. AI compresses tasks; it does not create free time on its own. If the twenty minutes you save on an email immediately refill with three more small tasks, you have gained nothing except a slightly busier day. The hours only become real when you consciously reassign them — to deep work, to sales, or, just as legitimately, to leaving the office on time in a country where many self-employed people do not take the holidays they are entitled to.

I expected AI to give me more hours. It gave me the same hours with less friction — the win only appeared once I started blocking the freed slots for real work.

A realistic ramp

Nobody reaches ten hours in week one. An honest trajectory for a solo business looks more like this:

  1. Month one: 2–3 hours. One or two workflows, usually inbox and first drafts, used consistently rather than experimented with once.
  2. Month two: 4–6 hours. Meeting notes, admin drafts and document search running as weekly routines.
  3. Month three and beyond: 8–10 hours. The routines run without you having to think about them, and the customer-communication hour appears.

Measure it honestly: keep a rough tally for two weeks before you start and two weeks after. Count only tasks the AI genuinely took over, and separate billable from administrative hours — an admin hour reinvested in client work is worth several times its face value.

What it costs to get there

One solid AI subscription plus perhaps a small add-on typically lands between CHF 20 and CHF 60 a month. Set against even a few reclaimed hours at a freelancer’s usual rate, the arithmetic is not close — but only if the reclaimed hours are real, which is why the tally matters more than the tool choice. For a systematic start, do a one-week time audit first: track where your hours actually go, then hand the biggest recurring annoyance to the AI before anything else.

LightCraft for Swiss SMEs: Edit Client Photos on Your Own Computer

Photo workflowData protectionSmall business

A product photo, a team portrait or a picture of completed work can make a small business look more trustworthy. Yet sending client or workplace photos to an online editor is not always comfortable. LightCraft is a free, open-source photo editor that runs on your computer, offering a way to develop and organise images without making a cloud service part of every edit.

What LightCraft does

LightCraft is designed for managing a photo library and adjusting photographs, including camera RAW files. You can organise images into folders or albums, compare shots, crop and straighten them, adjust light and colour, reduce noise, and export finished copies. Batch export and naming options can help when preparing several product images or a set of event photographs. Edits are non-destructive: the original image remains available while you refine the look.

This is a photo editor, not a magic image generator. The current feature list describes subject and sky selection as using traditional image cues for now, rather than a dedicated AI model. It also lists some advanced features as still in development. Check any automated selection and confirm that the functions you rely on are actually available.

Where it could help a small business

A craft seller might make the colour and brightness of product pictures consistent. A consultant could prepare a clear portrait for a website. A café or guesthouse could sort a batch of room or menu photographs before updating its site. LightCraft offers familiar adjustments without a subscription, and the project provides desktop releases for major computer platforms as well as a browser version.

That does not make it the right choice for every office. It is most useful if photographs matter to your work, you want more control than a phone filter gives, and someone has time to learn a new application. If you only crop an occasional picture, the editor already on your phone may be quicker. The software costs nothing, but setup, storage, learning and backup time are still real costs.

Local editing helps, but is not a privacy policy

Keeping the editing process on your own computer can avoid uploading an image to a third-party editing service. That matters if a photograph shows a client, a private room, a document in the background, or a location you do not want to disclose. It also means you can work without sending each image to an AI provider. This is a practical reduction in exposure, not proof that the whole device or application has passed an independent security audit.

Think about what happens before and after editing too. A shared computer, an automatic cloud backup or a public download link can expose the same photo. Images may also retain location or camera details. Use a work account with a screen lock, decide who can access the photo folder, keep a separate backup, and remove metadata when it is not needed for the job. Ask permission before publishing identifiable client or staff photographs.

Try it safely before changing your workflow

Begin with a copy of an ordinary product photo or an image you have permission to use. Import a small folder, make a few edits, export the result and check it on the website or device where customers will see it. Compare the exported file with the original, check the colours and crop, and confirm that the format and size meet your needs. Do not start with confidential client material or make a first experiment on the only copy of a deliverable.

  • Check the current release and system requirements before installing.
  • Keep original files and make a backup before a batch edit.
  • Test export quality, file size and metadata on your actual publishing channel.
  • Keep your established tool for specialist print work or any step LightCraft does not yet handle reliably.

LightCraft is worth a small, low-risk trial if you regularly prepare photos and prefer local tools. Its open-source license and broad platform availability are attractive, but a fast-moving project is not the same as a supported business service. Test the exact job you need, keep a fallback, and adopt it only if the finished images meet your standard.

Local AI on Your Laptop: A Beginner's Guide for Swiss Practices

Privacy Local AI Data

You do not need a subscription to use AI. A perfectly capable model can run on the laptop you already own — quietly, on your own hardware, with the data never leaving the room. For a Swiss notary, fiduciary or doctor, that is not a gimmick. It is the difference between sending a client file to a distant server and keeping it on the desk in front of you.

Local AI sounds technical, but the everyday version is simple. You install one small application, it downloads a model to your computer, and from then on you can summarise, draft and translate — offline, in private, without a monthly bill. This guide walks you through what you need, what works well, and where to start.

What local AI actually means

Most AI you already know — ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot — runs on servers you do not control. You send your text to a data centre, and an answer comes back. Local AI is the opposite: the model itself runs on your computer. Your document, your question and the answer all stay on your own machine.

A model is just a file — a few gigabytes of learned patterns. Once it sits on your disk, it behaves like any other program: you open it, use it, close it. Nothing is sent anywhere.

Is my laptop strong enough?

The honest answer is: for the small jobs, probably yes. The newer models are surprisingly light.

  • A Mac with an M1 chip or newer (from 2020) runs small models comfortably.
  • A Windows or Linux PC with 16 GB of memory and a recent graphics card handles the smaller models well.
  • A modest machine can still run a compact model for short summaries and drafts — it is just a little slower.

Start with a small model. If it feels too slow or too weak, you can always move up — but most first users are surprised how much a small model can already do.

The tools to start with

There are two friendly starting points, both free:

Ollama

Ollama is a small command you install, then type one line to download and run a model. It stays in the background and answers from a terminal window.

LM Studio

LM Studio is an app with a normal window, a search field for models and a chat-style interface — it feels familiar from the first minute.

Both run the same kind of models. Pick whichever feels more comfortable; you can switch later.

What local AI is good at — and what it is not

Be realistic and you will not be disappointed:

  • Good at: summarising documents, drafting emails and letters, proofreading, turning notes into clean text, translating between German, French and English.
  • Weaker at: the hardest reasoning, very long documents, or anything where a small mistake matters and no human checks the result.

A small local model is a diligent assistant, not a specialist. For routine office work — exactly the kind that eats your week — it is more than enough. For the final check, you are still the one in charge.

A first exercise: summarise a document

Here is a good first test, using a letter or a short contract already on your desk. Do not use a real client file yet — start with something harmless, like an insurance letter or an old meeting note.

Summarise this letter in five plain sentences. List the deadlines, the amounts and anything I need to do. Keep it in the same language as the letter.

Read the result. If it is clear and correct, you have just learned what the tool is for. If something is off, you have also learned something useful: where you still need to look yourself.

When local beats cloud, and when it does not

Choose local when:

  • the document contains professional secrecy, patient data or client details you would not email to a stranger;
  • you want privacy without reading a vendor's terms;
  • you want a fixed tool with no monthly fee.

Stay with a cloud tool when:

  • you need the strongest model for a hard, non-sensitive task;
  • you need a feature local tools do not yet offer;
  • the convenience of your team's current setup matters more.

Many practices settle on a middle path: local for the sensitive routine work, a cloud tool for the rest, and clear rules about which is which.

Data rules worth writing down

Local AI keeps your data on your machine, but the same habits still apply:

  • Keep the human in front — every draft is read by a person before it goes out.
  • Back up what matters — a local model will not save your files for you.
  • Stay current — update the app when it asks, so you run a maintained version.

One page, three lines, done. The point of local AI is less worry, not new paperwork.

The outcome

You can have a useful, private assistant running on the laptop you already own within an hour — no subscription, no data centre, no fuss. Start with one small model and one real task. Let it summarise, draft and tidy the routine work, keep the sensitive files at home, and you have taken the gentlest first step into AI there is.

Meta's New AI Agent for Small Businesses: Worth a Try?
