Meta just pushed its AI assistant, Muse, into the small-business world. It plugs into the tools you already use — Slack, Zoom, Canva, QuickBooks, Shopify, Stripe and more — and promises to save you hours. Here is what it actually does, and whether a Swiss SME should care.

What Muse for Small Business is

Muse is Meta’s AI agent, and the small-business version connects it to the software you already run your company with. Meta lists integrations with Asana, Box, Canva, Dropbox, Figma, Intuit QuickBooks, Notion, Shopify, Slack, Stripe, Zoom and others. The pitch is that, because Muse can see your tools, it has the context of your whole operation — what you sell, how your brand sounds, and the questions customers ask most — instead of being a blank chatbot that knows nothing about you.

The service is free with usage limits, and you pay for a subscription if you want more. Meta is clear about the target: owners who are short on hours, not on ideas.

What it can actually do for you

In practice, an agent like this is useful for the repetitive, low-stakes work that eats your evenings. Drafting replies, summarising a thread, turning a note into a to-do, finding a document, or writing a first version of an update to a customer. Because it sits inside the tools you already use, you do not have to copy and paste between a chatbot and your real work.

The honest limit is the same as with every agent: it is strong on drafting and summarising, and weaker on anything that needs your judgement. Let it write the first version; you make the call.

The part worth pausing over: your data

Muse is a cloud service run by Meta. Anything you let it read — customer names, order history, messages, financials — is processed on Meta’s infrastructure. That matters for a Swiss business in two ways. First, customer data has to stay protected under Swiss and European data-protection rules. Second, you are handing a very large company a detailed picture of how you do business.

None of this means you cannot use it. It means you should be deliberate: start with non-sensitive tasks, do not connect your accounting or customer files on day one, and treat anything you type as if it were going into a shared system.

Should you try it?

If you are curious, yes — start small. Pick one repetitive task, connect one tool, and run it for a week. Compare the time saved against the time spent checking its work. If it earns its place, keep it; if not, you have lost nothing.

The bigger picture is more interesting than any single tool: the big platforms are now betting that small businesses want an agent that knows their whole operation. Whether you use Meta’s version or a local one you run yourself, the useful habit is the same — hand the routine to a machine, and keep the judgement for yourself.

Microsoft Copilot for Swiss Teams: Start Small, Win Early

Management Meetings Automation

If your office already runs on Microsoft 365 — Outlook for mail, Teams for calls and chat, Word and Excel for the real work — then Copilot is not another tool to learn. It is a quiet layer over the tools your team already knows. The mistake most firms make is switching everything on at once and hoping for the best. The way is the opposite: start with one small win, and let it earn its place.

Copilot drafts, summarises and finds. It writes a first version of an email, recaps a meeting nobody had time to note, and pulls a half-remembered figure out of last month's chat. None of that replaces your team; it just removes the friction around the edges of the day.

Why start small

A rollout that dumps Copilot into every app at once creates noise. People get suggestions they did not ask for, and within a week the whole thing is switched off again. Starting small has three quiet advantages:

  • Trust is earned. Your team sees one useful result, then believes the next.
  • Cost stays honest. You learn what actually saves time before you commit more licences.
  • Habits stick. One good habit practised daily beats five half-learned features.

Three quiet first steps

Step 1 — Let it recap the meeting

The single most useful thing Copilot does in Teams is the meeting recap. After a call, it produces a short summary, a list of decisions and a list of open points. One person glances at it, corrects anything wrong, and posts it — instead of someone typing notes during the meeting and missing half the conversation.

Step 2 — Let it draft the follow-up email

In Outlook, Copilot drafts replies and new messages from a short instruction. You stay in control: the draft is only ever a starting point, and nothing goes out until you have read it.

Step 3 — Let it find the thing you half-remember

Copilot can search across your own mail, files and chats. Instead of scrolling through a long thread to find one address or one figure, you ask in plain words and it finds it.

A rollout: one feature per week

You do not need a project plan. Four quiet weeks are enough:

  • Week 1 — Meeting recaps only. Turn on recap in Teams, use it in every meeting, and correct the summaries out loud so people see how they should look.
  • Week 2 — Email drafts. One or two people draft their replies with Copilot and read every word before sending.
  • Week 3 — Search and catch-up. Show the team how to find files and catch up on missed chats.
  • Week 4 — Decide what stays. Keep the features that clearly save time, switch off the rest, and write one short line about the rules.

A prompt to start with

Give the tool a little context and it works far better. A useful first prompt for a follow-up email:

Draft a short, friendly follow-up email to a client after our meeting. We agreed I would send the offer by Friday. Keep it to three sentences, warm but not pushy, and leave the date open for their questions.

Read it, adjust the tone until it sounds like you, and send. That is the whole routine.

Data rules worth writing down

Copilot runs in Microsoft's cloud, so the usual care applies — the same care you already use with email and file storage:

  • Think before you paste. If you would not put a detail in a normal email, do not ask Copilot to handle it.
  • Keep sensitive cases local. For patient data, professional secrecy or client files under a duty of confidentiality, stay with the tools your practice already trusts, and keep the human decision in front.
  • Review before send. Every AI draft is read by a person. No exception.

For Swiss practices this is largely the same discipline the Data Protection Act asks of you anyway: know which tools you use, for what, and with which data.

What Copilot is not

It is not a colleague, and it is not a decision-maker. It does not understand your clients, and it will occasionally get a fact wrong. Treat its output as a competent first draft — useful precisely because you are the one who finishes it.

The outcome

One month, three small habits, and the daily friction — typing the same emails, hunting for lost information, reconstructing what a meeting decided — quietly shrinks. You do not need to be an AI pioneer. You just need to start small, in the tools you already use, and let the tool prove itself one week at a time.

Stay Top of Mind with Clients: An AI Routine for Your Monthly Newsletter

Newsletter Clients Marketing

A fiduciary in Zug finishes a client's tax return and the relationship quietly goes quiet. A doctor in Lausanne treats a patient, and by the next quarter the patient has forgotten her name. A notary in Bern does excellent work, but when a past client needs legal help again, they cannot remember who to call. In every case the problem is the same: out of sight, out of mind.

For a small Swiss practice, the most valuable asset is trust built over years — but trust needs a gentle reminder now and then. A short monthly newsletter is the gentlest way to stay present in your clients' lives without selling, pushing or chasing. And with AI handling the mechanical parts, it takes half an hour a month, not a whole afternoon.

Why a newsletter works better than you think

Most self-employed people assume a newsletter means marketing, a mailing list and hours of writing. It does not have to. A quiet monthly note does three useful things:

  • It is permission-based and low-pressure. People signed up, so a monthly note feels welcome, not pushy.
  • It compounds quietly. One useful note a month, and after a year your clients think of you first when something comes up.
  • It is reusable. One topic can become an email, a LinkedIn post and a short page on your website.

A simple routine that takes 30 minutes

You do not need to become a writer or a marketer. You need a simple, repeatable routine that you can run once a month, in a quiet half hour, without stress.

Step 1 — Collect three small topics (5 minutes)

Note down what happened this month: a change in the law, a common client question, a small tip, or a deadline worth flagging. You do not need a big idea; useful beats clever every time.

Step 2 — Let the AI draft the newsletter

Give the AI your three topics and a couple of sentences about your practice. Ask for a short, warm newsletter in your voice.

Write a short monthly newsletter for my [notary / fiduciary / medical] practice in [language]. Tone: warm, plain, no marketing hype, no exclamation marks. Structure: a one-line greeting, three short paragraphs (one per topic below), and a closing line with a soft invitation to get in touch. Under 200 words. Topics: [paste your three topics].

Step 3 — Review, personalise, send

Read the draft once, add one personal detail (a seasonal greeting, a local note), check the names and dates, and send. Five minutes of review, and the whole thing is done.

Where to find topics without effort

The hardest part is usually deciding what to write about. Here is where the material hides:

  • Common client questions. The answer you give three times a week is a newsletter topic.
  • Legal and tax changes. Flag them before your clients ask — that is exactly when they trust you most.
  • Seasonal deadlines. Renewal dates, filing dates, check-up reminders. Useful, timely, easy to write.
  • A small note about your practice. A new team member, new opening hours, a short holiday notice.

Keep a simple running list. Whenever a client asks a good question or a deadline approaches, add a line to the list. At the end of the month, pick three.

What AI does well — and what stays with you

  • The blank page: the AI turns three bullet points into flowing, readable text.
  • Consistency: the same warm voice every month, even when you are busy.
  • The translations: if you serve clients in German, French and English, the AI can draft all three versions in minutes.

What stays with you is the judgement: which topics matter, what your clients actually need, and what you would never say. The AI drafts; you decide. That division never changes.

A note on data and privacy

A newsletter is generic, so there is usually nothing confidential in it. But keep individual client data — names, amounts, medical details — out of the draft. Describe the audience, not specific people. If you ever need to paste a client list or a case into a draft, use a local or zero-retention service instead of a public chatbot.

The outcome

Once a month, every client hears from you in a useful way. Referrals come more easily, past clients return, and you stop worrying about "marketing" because the newsletter does it quietly in the background. Thirty minutes a month, and you stay present without ever chasing anyone.

Know Where Your Business Stands Every Month

Monthly reviewBusiness overviewReporting

Running a business and understanding it are two different jobs. Most self-employed people have their numbers somewhere — in a bank account, an invoice folder, a bookkeeping tool — but rarely in one place where the whole picture is visible. This routine gives you a short monthly summary of where your business actually stands.

Gather the numbers once a month

Pick a fixed day — the first Monday, the last Friday, whichever suits you — and spend fifteen minutes pulling together the basics: money in, money out, invoices sent, invoices still open, and any large expenses.

You do not need perfect bookkeeping for this. Rough figures are enough to see the direction of travel. If the numbers live in a tool, export them; if they live in your head, write them down.

Hand these figures to an AI tool and ask for a plain-language summary: one page, no jargon, three or four key numbers and what they mean.

Keep a simple template so the process is the same every month. The less you have to think about how to gather the numbers, the more likely you are to actually do it.

Ask the right questions

The quality of the summary depends on the questions you ask. Instead of “summarise my month”, try: what came in, what went out, what is still owed to me, and what surprised you about this month.

Ask the AI to compare with the previous month, so you can see whether things are moving up, down, or staying flat. Trends matter more than single numbers.

Keep the summary short. If it runs longer than a page, it is no longer a summary — it is a report, and you will not read it.

Turn the summary into one decision

A summary is only useful if it changes something. At the end of each monthly read, pick one small action: chase one overdue invoice, cancel one unused expense, or set one goal for next month.

Write that single action at the top of the summary, so it is the first thing you see next time. Over a year, twelve small actions add up to a very different business.

Do not let the summary grow a life of its own. One action per month is enough. If you try to fix everything at once, nothing gets fixed.

  1. Pull the numbers.
  2. Ask for a one-page summary.
  3. Note the trend versus last month.
  4. Choose one action and write it down.

What you gain

You stop guessing how the month went and start knowing. You catch problems early, while they are still small and cheap to fix. And you build a quiet habit of steering your business instead of just reacting to it.

This routine costs a quarter of an hour a month and gives back a clearer head the rest of the time. That is a good trade. After a few months, the trend lines start to tell a story of their own.

Writing to Clients in Their Own Language: AI for German, French and English Letters

LanguagesCorrespondenceClients

A notary in Fribourg drafts a contract for a client who has always written in French. A doctor in Biel answers a patient in whichever language the patient prefers. A fiduciary in Lugano prepares a report that a client in Zurich will read. In Switzerland, writing well means writing in the client's language — and getting it slightly wrong reads as carelessness.

This article describes a simple routine for client correspondence in German, French and English. The AI helps you draft the message in the client's language so it reads naturally, not like machine translation. You stay in control of every word and every tone. No new software project — just a short prompt and a little care before you press send.

Why the client's language matters

Language in Switzerland is not just a means of communication; it is a form of respect. A client who receives a letter in their own language feels understood. A client who receives a clumsy translation quietly wonders what else was handled carelessly.

  • Trust is local: a fiduciary who writes fluent French to a client in Geneva signals that the relationship matters.
  • Small mistakes read loudly: one wrong gender, one anglicism, one sentence translated word for word, and the client starts to doubt the details they cannot see.
  • Tone does not translate on its own: a polite Swiss-German phrase does not always become a polite French one. The AI helps you carry the meaning, not just the words.

A three-step routine

Step 1 — Write the message in your own words

Start in the language you think in. Write down what you want to say, roughly, without worrying about elegance. The AI's job is the language, not the content — the facts, the numbers and the decisions stay yours.

Here is what I want to tell my client. Rewrite it in clear, polite French (Swiss French, informal « tu »). Keep the meaning and the structure, but make it sound as if a real person from this region wrote it. Do not add anything I did not say. Avoid anglicisms — use « réunion », « offre », « facture », « clients ».

Step 2 — Ask for natural phrasing, not a translation

This is the step that separates a useful draft from a wooden one: ask the AI to write, not to translate. Translation produces literal, stiff sentences. Asking the AI to write the way a native speaker would produces a message a real client would not even notice.

Read this German letter I drafted. Rewrite it in natural Swiss German (informal « du », no ß, no anglicisms — « Offerte », « Sitzung », « Pendenzen », « Kunden »). Keep it no urgency, no « sofort ». Preserve all the facts and the friendly tone.

Step 3 — Read it back in your own language

Before you send, ask the AI to translate the finished message back into your own language. This « back-translation » is your safety net: you read it to confirm that nothing was added, dropped or subtly changed. If the meaning survived the round trip, the letter is ready.

What the AI is good at — and what it is not

An AI is genuinely helpful here: it carries tone, chooses phrasing a native speaker would recognise, and remembers to avoid the anglicisms that quietly mark a text as foreign. It is patient and never gets tired of drafting the same polite paragraph twice.

It is not a substitute for your judgement. It does not know your client's history, your private shorthand, or the legal nuance behind a sentence. And it cannot know what you deliberately left unsaid. Treat it as a careful colleague who writes well in three languages but decides nothing.

A note on data

Client letters contain names, amounts and sometimes health or legal context, so the usual data-protection rules apply. Use a business-grade tool rather than a private consumer account, check whether the provider stores your input or trains on it, and anonymise first if you are unsure — replace names and figures with placeholders, draft the message, then add the real details back at the end.

The outcome

The goal is a letter your client reads without noticing the language — which is, quietly, the highest compliment a Swiss professional can receive. Start with the next message to a client in another language region. Three steps, one prompt, and every client hears from you in their own words.

NanoClaw: A WhatsApp AI Assistant That Only Sees Its Own Conversations

AI AgentsData protectionClient Communication

Imagine an assistant that quietly answers your WhatsApp while you sit with a client. This week the open-source project NanoClaw drew attention because of the story behind it: its author discovered that his previous AI assistant had been silently reading every WhatsApp group on his account — including chats full of other people’s details. So he rebuilt it around one rule: the assistant only ever sees the conversation it is working on. That story is worth more to a Swiss small business than any feature list.

What NanoClaw actually is

NanoClaw is a small, free program that you run yourself. Once set up, it connects an AI — Anthropic’s Claude — to WhatsApp, Telegram, Slack, Discord and Gmail. From inside a chat you can ask questions, draft messages, set reminders or run small searches, without opening a laptop.

Two things make it unusual. First, it is tiny: the core is roughly 500 lines of code, readable in minutes. Comparable assistants are far bigger — the popular OpenClaw is reported to run past 400,000 lines, which nobody outside the project ever fully reads. Second, every conversation runs in its own sealed container — a locked room inside your computer. The assistant never sees your raw access keys and cannot wander into the rest of your machine.

In everyday terms: instead of handing an assistant the keys to your whole office, you let it work in one room, with one drawer.

Why the backstory matters more than the features

The author, developer Gavriel Cohen, wrote the first version in a weekend — 48 hours after realising his old assistant had been reading every group on his WhatsApp the whole time. Not because the tool was malicious, but because nothing had stopped it. Client names, order details, private conversations of people who never agreed to any AI reading along: all of it lay open to a program.

For a Swiss business, that lesson lands twice as hard. Under the revised Swiss data protection law you remain responsible for client data even when a tool processes it for you. And group chats are full of other people’s information — customers, staff, family — who never chose your AI assistant. NanoClaw’s strict separation is its answer to exactly that: one chat, one sealed box, no keys to anything else.

The honest costs and limits

A free tool is not a free lunch. Before you get excited, count what it takes:

  • You install and maintain it yourself. It is not an app from a store; it runs inside Docker, a sealed workshop for software. The project itself says a first setup takes 30 to 60 minutes.
  • The AI is not included. You connect your own Claude API key, and every processed message costs a small amount on Anthropic’s bill. Light use stays cheap, but the centimes add up.
  • The sandbox protects your machine, not the chat itself. When the AI “thinks” about a message, that still happens in Anthropic’s cloud — chat content still leaves your computer while it is being processed.
  • WhatsApp has strict rules. WhatsApp officially allows automated sending only through its own Business API. Third-party bridges sit in a grey zone and can, at worst, cost you your number — a real risk on a channel your clients use.

What to take with you, even if you never install it

Most readers will not spend a weekend on Docker — and that is fine. The value of the story is the checklist behind it. Before you connect any AI tool to your client communication, ask:

  1. What exactly can it read — one conversation, or everything?
  2. Where does the content go while it is processed — your computer, or a cloud abroad?
  3. What is it allowed to do — only draft, or send on its own?
  4. Who else appears in those conversations, and did they agree?
  5. Can you switch it off cleanly, and delete what it saw?

If a WhatsApp assistant ever lands on your wishlist, start small: a test number, a dummy chat, nothing client-facing in the first month. And if you connect nothing at all — this checklist still applies to the next tool that promises to answer your messages for you.

Never Miss a Deadline: An AI Routine for Legal and Tax Dates

DeadlinesRemindersPlanning

A notary in Lucerne has a contract registration deadline next Tuesday. A fiduciary in Basel has the MWST quarter closing this week. A doctor in Geneva promised a patient a report by Friday. None of them will miss it on purpose — the danger is that the date quietly slides past, buried in an email, a letter or a sticky note.

This article describes a simple routine for keeping every legal, tax and renewal date on one list — and letting the AI handle the sorting, the reminders and the first draft of the follow-ups. You stay in control of every decision. Nothing is automated behind your back.

The idea is not another app to check. It is one list and one short weekly habit — supported by AI, but run by you.

Why deadlines get missed

It is rarely carelessness. It is usually structure. Dates arrive scattered across many places, and nothing brings them together:

  • No single list: deadlines live in emails, letters, contracts and a calendar that nobody fully trusts.
  • Set-and-forget: a date is noted once, then never resurfaces until it is too late to act.
  • Too late a warning: the reminder arrives the day before, when the preparation needed weeks.

For a notary, a missed Frist can mean liability. For a fiduciary, a missed MWST date means a penalty. For a doctor, a late report erodes trust. The cost is real — and it is almost always avoidable.

A three-step routine

Step 1 — Collect every date into one list

Once, gather every deadline you know about: legal Fristen, tax and MWST dates, contract renewals, permit expiries, report promises. Put them into a simple list — a note, a spreadsheet, a document. Each entry only needs a date, a short name and a lead time (how many days before the date you want to start).

Step 2 — Let the AI sort and schedule

Hand the list to the AI and ask it to turn it into a forward schedule. The AI reads the lead times and works backwards: this report must start today, this renewal can wait until next month.

Here is my list of deadlines with dates and lead times. Sort them by the date I need to start acting, not by the deadline itself. For each, tell me the earliest sensible start date and what the first step is. Keep it clear and simple — no urgency, no « sofort ».

Step 3 — The weekly ten-minute review

Pick one fixed slot each week — ten minutes is enough. You review the coming two weeks, move anything that has changed, and let the AI draft the reminders and follow-ups you will actually send. This single habit is what turns a good list into a system that does not fail.

Let the AI draft the follow-up, not just the alarm

The useful part is not the reminder itself. It is the message that comes with it: the polite nudge to a client whose document is still missing, the note to a colleague, the internal checklist for a report. The AI drafts it; you approve it.

Draft a short, friendly reminder to my client in Swiss German (informal « du », no anglicisms). Their signed contract copy is still missing and I need it by Friday. Keep it friendly, one short paragraph, no pressure.

What this looks like for your profession

  • Notaries and law firms: registration and submission Fristen, contract milestones, notarisation dates.
  • Fiduciaries: MWST and tax deadlines, annual statements, payroll dates, client document deadlines.
  • Doctors and small offices: report promises, insurance and permit renewals, follow-up appointments.

One quiet hour to set it up, ten minutes a week to maintain it, and the number of dates that slip through drops to nearly zero. The Problem with "Find and Replace"

Most legal professionals survive on a library of old files and Ctrl+F. But this manual assembly line has hidden costs:

  • The "Ghost Client" Risk: Accidentally leaving the previous client's name or address on page 14 of a contract.
  • Context Switching: Jumping between the client intake email, the ID scans, and the Word document.
  • Lost Billable Hours: Routine assembly takes time away from complex advisory work that clients actually value.

The AI-Assisted Assembly Line

This is exactly the type of friction modern AI models are built to eliminate. You don't need a massive, expensive legal-tech software suite to fix this. You need a simple, secure workflow.

Step 1: The Intake Summary

Instead of manually extracting data from client emails, you can use a local or secure enterprise AI model to summarize the intake. You provide the email thread and a prompt: "Extract the names, addresses, ID numbers, and key transaction details from these emails into a structured list."

Step 2: The Template Injection

You provide the AI with your pristine, blank master template (with placeholders like [CLIENT_A_NAME]) and the extracted data. The AI does the heavy lifting of injecting the right data into the right clauses, adjusting pronouns, and ensuring formatting consistency.

For Swiss legal professionals (who are bound by strict professional secrecy under Art. 321 SCC), pasting client data into a public ChatGPT window is an absolute non-starter.

The solution is not to avoid AI, but to use the right architecture:

  • Local LLMs: Running models directly on your office hardware. The data never leaves your computer.
  • Zero-Data-Retention Enterprise APIs: Using providers (like specific tiers of Microsoft Azure Switzerland or Anthropic) with strict, legally binding zero-retention agreements where your data is processed but never stored or used for training.
  • Anonymization First: Using AI to draft the complex structure of the contract using placeholder names (John Doe, Muster AG), and doing a final manual "Find and Replace" with the real names offline.

Your One-Page AI Policy: Clear Rules for Notaries, Fiduciaries and Doctors

Compliance Data Privacy Policy

Every Swiss practice that uses AI — a notary's office, a fiduciary, a doctor's surgery, a small firm — slowly builds a list of tools: a dictation assistant here, a summariser there, a chatbot for drafting letters. One day someone asks a simple question: "What exactly do we use AI for here, and where does the data go?" If you cannot answer that in thirty seconds, you need a one-page AI policy.

This is not bureaucracy for its own sake. It is the sensible way to know, at a glance, which tools are allowed, for which tasks, and with which data — and to show that to a client, an employee or an auditor without a scramble.

Why one page is enough

A policy that no one reads is worse than no policy. The goal is not a thick manual; it is a single page that anyone in the practice can understand in two minutes. It answers four questions:

  • Which tools? The named services you actually use — the dictation app, the translation assistant, the email drafter.
  • For what? The tasks where AI is welcome, and the ones where it is not.
  • With which data? What may be pasted in, and what must stay out — client names, patient data, figures.
  • Who decides? The human checks every AI draft before it goes out. No exception.

A simple routine to write it

You do not need a lawyer or a consultant to draft the first version. You need one quiet hour and a simple prompt. Give the AI your real situation and let it propose a structure, then you shorten it until it fits on one page.

Step 1 — List what you actually use

Sit down and write out every AI tool anyone in the practice touches in a normal week. Be honest and complete: the dictation software on the phone, the summariser in the meeting app, the chatbot someone uses for letters. This list is the backbone of the policy.

Step 2 — Let the AI draft the page

Hand the AI your list and a few sentences about your data, and ask it to draft the page in plain language:

We are a small Swiss practice (a notary / a fiduciary / a medical office). We use the following AI tools: [list them]. We work with personal and sometimes sensitive data (client files, health data, figures). Please draft a one-page internal AI policy in plain language that covers: (1) which tools are approved, (2) which tasks AI may be used for, (3) which data may never be entered, (4) that every AI draft must be reviewed by a human before it is sent, and (5) a short note on our obligations under the Swiss Data Protection Act. Keep it to one page, in clear sentences, without legal jargon.

Step 3 — Shorten, sign and pin it up

Read the draft once, cut anything vague, and check that the four questions are answered. Then date it, share it with the team, and pin a copy where people actually see it. Review it once a year, or whenever you add a new tool.

A second prompt: the client-ready sentence

Clients are starting to ask how their data is handled. You do not need a long answer — one honest sentence is enough. Ask the AI to turn your policy into it:

From our one-page AI policy, write one sentence for clients explaining that we use AI to help with drafting and organisation, that sensitive data is never entered into public tools, and that a person always reviews the final result.

What the page does for you

  • Clarity for the team. Everyone knows what is allowed, so no one improvises with client data.
  • Trust with clients. You answer the data question in one sentence instead of hesitating.
  • in an audit. You can show, in writing, that AI use is deliberate and documented.

What it is not

A one-page policy is not a substitute for the law, and it is not a guarantee. It is a record of intent and a shared rule. For anything involving sensitive patient data, professional secrecy, or large contracts, the careful step remains: use local or zero-retention tools, and keep the human decision in front.

The outcome

One quiet hour, one page, and the question "what do we use AI for here?" finally has a written answer. You pin it up, forget about it for a year, and get back to the work you are actually good at.

Never Let an Offer Go Cold: An AI Routine for Following Up on Open Quotes

Offers Sales Clients

A fiduciary in Zurich sends a careful offer for a new client's bookkeeping — and hears nothing for three weeks. A notary in Lausanne quotes for a property transfer, and the file stays silent. A small medical practice offers a corporate health package, and the phone never rings. In every case the work is already done: the quote was written, priced and sent. What is missing is not effort — it is follow-up.

Open offers are one of the quietest leaks in a small Swiss practice. Every unanswered quote is time you already invested, with nothing to show for it. The good news is that a once-a-week AI routine turns that silent pile into a short, friendly follow-up list — and a noticeably higher closing rate, without ever chasing or pushing.

Why offers go quiet

Almost no unanswered offer means a clear "no". Most of the time the answer is really "not yet" — and the reason is usually one of these:

  • The timing is off. The client asked for a quote during a busy week and has not found a quiet moment to look at it.
  • The offer got buried. It sits under forty newer emails and never surfaces again.
  • The client is comparing. They asked two or three providers and are waiting to hear back from all of them.
  • Something is unclear. A price, a scope, a date — but asking feels like too much effort.

None of these mean no. Most of them mean "help me decide". That is exactly what a follow-up does. A quiet follow-up costs you three minutes and gives the client a gentle nudge at the right moment — most of the time, that is all it takes.

A weekly routine in three steps

You do not need a CRM or a sales process. You need one quiet half hour a week and a simple, repeatable routine.

Step 1 — Collect your open offers (10 minutes)

Go through the quotes you sent in the last few weeks and list the ones without an answer: the client, the date, the subject and the amount. Put them in a simple list — a note, a spreadsheet, or even a piece of paper.

Step 2 — Let the AI draft, you decide

Hand the list to the AI and ask for a short, friendly follow-up for each one. Give it your tone and a couple of rules.

You are helping me follow up on open offers. Below is a list of quotes I sent with no answer, with the client, the date and the subject. For each one, write a short, warm follow-up in [language]. Tone: friendly, no pressure, no discount unless I ask. Keep each message under 80 words, and end with a soft question that is easy to answer. List: [paste your list].

Step 3 — Send and note the answer

Read each draft once, add one personal line if you like, and send. Then note the reply — or the silence — and set the date for the next follow-up. The routine takes ten more minutes and keeps the whole list moving.

A gentle sequence that never feels like chasing

One message is often not enough, but three messages feel like pressure. A sequence of three touches, spaced a few days apart, works better:

  • Touch 1 (a few days after sending): "Did you have a chance to look at the offer? Happy to answer any questions."
  • Touch 2 (about a week later): Add one useful detail — a clarification, a date, a small point that helps the decision.
  • Touch 3 (one close): "I'll close the file at the end of the week if I don't hear back — no problem at all."

The third message sounds counterintuitive, but it works: it removes the pressure and gives the client a clear, gentle exit. Many people answer exactly then.

What AI does well — and what stays with you

  • The first draft: the AI turns a dry list of offers into warm, natural follow-ups in the right language.
  • Consistency: the same friendly tone every week, even when you are busy.
  • The translations: if a client writes in French and you answer in German, the AI keeps the follow-up in the client's language.

What stays with you is the judgement: who deserves a follow-up, what the right tone is for each client, and when to stop. The AI drafts; you decide. That division never changes.

A note on data and privacy

An offer list contains names and amounts, so keep it away from public chatbots unless you anonymise first. Use first names or initials, describe the subject instead of quoting the whole document, and leave out anything sensitive. If a client or a case must be named, use a local or zero-retention service instead of a public window.

The outcome

One quiet half hour a week, and no offer silently expires again. A few more clients answer, a few more mandates come back to life, and you stop wondering whether "no answer" meant "no". It never feels like chasing, because it is not — it is simply remembering, politely, that you are still there.

An AI assistant usually waits for a question. OpenDots aims to be more like a named coworker: it can remember previous work, use a browser or files, and carry out a task on a computer. But OpenDots is an early open-source project, not a ready-made office service. The sensible question is not whether it can do everything; it is whether one small, supervised task is worth testing.

What OpenDots actually does

OpenDots lets you create a persistent AI teammate with a role. it can keep context between sessions. The project describes ways to talk to it by text or voice, and to connect it to Slack. Its computer can open a browser, work with files and run commands to complete a task.

A teammate might gather details from an approved folder, prepare a first draft, or organise information for a person to review. The project also describes approval pauses before actions such as saving or sending something. Those are product claims from the project, not an independent safety certification.

OpenDots is an MIT-licensed template that you host yourself. It does not include its own AI model: you must connect a compatible model service, and Slack use needs Slack credentials. Hosting the application yourself does not automatically mean the model, logs or every piece of data stay on your own computer.

Where it might help a small office

Start with work that is repetitive, easy to check and reversible. For example, an assistant could prepare a daily list of unanswered enquiries from a folder you have chosen, or draft a polite reply using a short set of approved answers. A person should check names, dates, promises and attachments before anything leaves the office.

Do not begin by giving it access to every mailbox, client folder or calendar. Choose one low-risk process and write down what a good result looks like. For a first trial, keep the agent in draft mode: it may prepare work, but a human performs the final send, booking or record change.

  • Pick one task that currently takes a few minutes each day.
  • Give access only to the files and accounts needed for that task.
  • Keep a person responsible for checking and approving the result.

Approval is useful, but not the whole security plan

A confirmation button can prevent an unwanted message from being sent. It cannot by itself prevent the agent from seeing more information than it should, making a misleading draft, or passing client details to the model service. Nor does a pause prove that every action is logged or can be undone.

Before using real business information, find out who operates the server and model, where information is processed, how long prompts and logs are retained, and who can access them. Check the project maturity too: its own description calls it alpha, says it is for a single owner, and notes that shared editing is not yet available. Voice and Slack delegation still need more real-world verification.

For a Swiss practice handling health, legal or financial information, use synthetic examples first. Ask your IT provider or data-protection adviser to review the setup and the relevant service terms. If you cannot explain where a client message goes, do not connect that mailbox yet.

A sensible way to decide

OpenDots is worth watching if you have technical support and want to experiment with a supervised digital helper. It is not the quick, plug-in solution its coworker metaphor might suggest: someone must host it, connect a model, set permissions and keep it updated. A paid hosted assistant may be simpler,

Try a small, non-sensitive pilot for a week. Track minutes saved, corrections needed and any moments when the agent asked for more access than expected. Stop if the human review takes as long as doing the task yourself, or if the data path is unclear. Keep the useful idea — a helper that prepares work and waits for approval — even if OpenDots itself is not yet right for your office.

From Payslip to Lohnausweis: An AI Routine for Payroll and Social Insurance

The moment a small Swiss office hires its first employee, a quiet pile of paperwork appears: AHV, BVG, accident insurance, source tax — and once a year, the Lohnausweis. None of it is intellectually hard, but all of it is deadline-driven and easy to get slightly wrong.

The truth is that payroll is not a mystery — it is a short list of repeating steps with a few fiddly details. And the fiddly details are exactly what AI handles well: gathering the month's changes, checking them against the rules, and drafting the message that goes to your payroll provider or accountant.

Why payroll quietly eats your time

Payroll rarely fails loudly. It fails quietly, through small omissions that surface weeks later as a correction, a phone call or a penalty notice:

  • Many institutions. One employee triggers obligations towards AHV/IV/EO, the pension fund (BVG), accident insurance (UVG/NBU) and, for cross-border or foreign staff, source tax.
  • Many deadlines. Contributions are due monthly or quarterly, and the annual statements follow their own calendar.
  • The annual Lohnausweis. The salary certificate you issue every January has fields that are genuinely easy to fill in wrongly, and a wrong figure lands straight in the employee's tax return.

What a small office actually has to track

Strip away the forms and payroll is a short list of facts that change each month:

  • Changes: new hires, departures, salary changes, hours, absences, bonuses.
  • Insurances: who is covered by BVG and UVG, and at what salary level.
  • Source tax: whether any employee is taxed at source, and at which rate.
  • The salary statements: the monthly payslip and the annual Lohnausweis.

An AI routine to run it

Step 1 — Keep a master sheet

Write down your own payroll facts once — the institutions, the contribution accounts, the deadline calendar and the salary levels that trigger BVG and UVG. This is the part that never changes and the part most likely to contain a typo if you look it up fresh every month.

Step 2 — Collect the month's changes in one note

Each month, jot the changes in a single short note: who joined, who left, who changed hours, any bonus or absence. Then hand the note and your master sheet to the AI:

You are helping a small Swiss office prepare its monthly payroll. Here is my master sheet: [institutions, accounts, salary levels, deadline calendar]. Here are this month's changes: [list]. Please draft the message to our payroll provider with the changes, and flag anything that affects AHV, BVG, accident insurance or source tax.

Step 3 — Let the AI draft, you approve

The AI does not pay anyone and does not transmit anything. It drafts the message and flags what looks off. You read it once, correct what needs correcting, and send it — the same way you would with a careful colleague.

A second prompt: checking the numbers

Before you send, run one more pass to catch the kind of mistake that turns into a correction:

Check this payroll message for common Swiss mistakes: is every new hire covered by the right insurances, are the BVG and UVG thresholds respected, is any employee subject to source tax, and are the amounts consistent with last month? List anything that looks wrong or missing.

The Lohnausweis at year-end

Every January the same question returns: the salary certificate. The Lohnausweis has a specific field for almost everything — gross salary, contributions, expense allowances, benefits in kind — and each field has its rules.

Here the AI earns its keep as a second pair of eyes. Give it last year's Lohnausweis, the twelve monthly summaries, and the current instructions, and ask it to draft the new certificate field by field, flagging anything that differs from the previous year and anything that needs your decision.

The result is not a finished document you sign blindly. It is a first draft you can review carefully, instead of a blank form at the end of January.

One honest caveat

The AI does not calculate contributions, does not file with the institutions, and does not replace your payroll provider or fiduciary. It drafts, checks and reminds — the mechanical parts that consume your time. The final responsibility for the numbers stays with you, exactly as it should.

The outcome

One master sheet, one monthly note, two short prompts, and one pass over the year-end certificate. Payroll stops being a monthly dread and becomes a routine you can finish in a quiet half-hour — and the Lohnausweis is ready before the rush, because the draft was already waiting.

PdfCraft is the opposite — a free, open-source PDF editor that runs entirely on your own computer. No account, no telemetry, no upload: your client documents stay where they belong.

If you have ever dropped a client’s contract into a free online PDF tool just to merge two files, you have met the problem. “Free” web tools usually mean your document travels to a server you know nothing about — sometimes outside Switzerland, sometimes outside Europe. For a notary, a fiduciary or a doctor, that is not a small detail. It is a data-protection decision made in a hurry.

Why the cloud question matters more than it sounds

Under the revised Swiss Data Protection Act, you stay responsible for client data even when a tool processes it for you — and professional confidentiality does not pause because a website promises “files deleted after one hour”. The safest transfer is the one that never happens. A good rule of thumb: if you would not post a copy of a document to a stranger, do not upload it to one either.

That is what makes a local editor interesting. It is not about distrust; it is about defaults. When a tool simply has no way to send your files anywhere, you stop reading privacy policies for routine jobs like merging, splitting or reordering pages.

What PdfCraft does well

PdfCraft is a young open-source project with apps for Windows, macOS and Linux. The everyday jobs it already covers well:

  • Reordering pages: drag pages around like cards — put a signed contract back in the right order before it goes to the client.
  • Merging and splitting: combine a week of scans into one clean dossier file, or split a thick scan into separate documents per topic.
  • Deep undo: changes are saved alongside the original instead of over it, so the bytes of an important file stay intact — a quiet form of insurance.
  • Damaged files: pages are rendered one by one, so a broken scan gets repaired rather than refused.

The program costs nothing, and the source code is public — anyone can check what it does instead of trusting a marketing page.

What it cannot do yet

An honest look includes the limits. Text recognition for scans (OCR) is not built in — you download a separate model first, and only you can judge whether its quality is good enough. Editing existing text inside a PDF is still at an early stage by the project’s own account. And if your daily work depends on professional redaction or qualified electronic signatures, keep your current tool for those jobs.

Take the project’s own numbers with calm as well: statements like “zero crashes on our test corpus” are the developers’ tests, not an independent audit. For routine page work on copies, that is fine. For the only copy of an original document, keep backups — as with any tool.

How to try it safely

  1. Take it from the source. Use the project’s own GitHub releases, not a random download portal that may bundle extra software.
  2. Work on copies first. Give it duplicates of real documents for a week — never the only copy of anything.
  3. Start with one routine. Pick a recurring job, such as merging the week’s scans every Friday, and let the new tool own just that one.
  4. Keep originals untouched. PdfCraft’s append-style saving helps, but your folder discipline matters more than any feature.

The quiet financial upside

There is also a plain cost argument. A mainstream PDF subscription runs roughly 15 to 25 dollars per user per month. For a three-person office, that is several hundred francs a year for tasks a free local tool covers just as well. Nobody has to switch overnight — simply stop paying for the jobs that never needed the cloud in the first place.

Data protection is often mostly a question of which tools you reach for. A local PDF editor will not make headlines, but it removes a whole category of risk from your week — quietly, and for free.

From Phone Call to Follow-Up: An AI Routine for Calls and Voicemails

Phone Workflow Clients

A notary in Zurich is in a client meeting when the phone rings. A fiduciary in Bern steps out for lunch and comes back to three missed calls and a full voicemail box. A doctor's receptionist scribbles "Herr Meier called about his test results" on a yellow sticky note. By Friday, nobody remembers who was supposed to call whom back.

For notaries, fiduciaries, doctors and small offices, the phone is still where a lot of the real work begins. A client calls with a question, a colleague calls with an update, a bank calls with a request, a cantonal office calls about a deadline. Each call is a promise to do something — and that promise is easy to lose the moment you hang up.

You do not need to answer every call on the spot or write perfect notes by hand. You need a way to capture each call, turn it into a short next step, and make sure nothing quietly disappears.

Why phone calls quietly cause trouble

The problem is rarely the calls themselves. It is that they arrive in bursts, between other tasks, and leave no trace unless you make one:

  • No written record: a call about a deadline or a sum of money exists only in your memory — and memory fades fast.
  • Sticky notes scatter: names, numbers and half-finished notes end up on different slips, none of them in the client file.
  • The callback falls through: you intend to call back "later", but later fills up and the promise is forgotten.

The cost shows up quietly: a client who waits too long, a deadline that slips past, a question that never gets answered.

A simple routine in three steps

You do not need a call-centre system. Three quiet steps, once a day or right after each call, are enough.

Step 1 — Capture the call

After a call, spend thirty seconds noting the essentials in your own words — or, where it is allowed and sensible, record the call and let the AI transcribe it. A few short lines are enough: who called, what it was about, what was agreed, and what needs to happen next.

Step 2 — Let the AI turn it into a next step

Hand the note or transcript to a secure AI setup and let it do the sorting. One prompt is enough:

Here is my note from a phone call with a client. Turn it into a short summary, then list: what was agreed, what I need to do next and by when, and what the client is expecting from me. Draft a short follow-up email to the client confirming the outcome and the next step. Keep the tone friendly, and never invent details — if something is unclear, mark it "to check".

Step 3 — One line in the client file, one follow-up sent

The result is a single, tidy entry: a one-line summary for the client file, a clear action for your to-do list, and a drafted follow-up email you can read, adjust and send. The call stops living in your head and becomes a small, finished piece of work.

Voicemails, without the dread

The voicemail box is where requests go to pile up. A prompt turns a full box into a short, sorted list instead:

Here are the transcribed voicemail messages from today. For each one, tell me: who called, what they need, whether it is urgent, and what action it requires from me. Sort them by priority and draft a short reply for each. Anything that is just advertising or a wrong number goes into a separate "ignore" list.

Ten minutes in the evening is often enough to empty the box, answer the urgent ones and quietly close the rest.

What AI does well — and what stays with you

  • Transcribing and summarising: turning a spoken call into clean written notes.
  • Extracting the action item: the one thing that must happen next, with a date.
  • Drafting the follow-up: a short, friendly message the client can reply to.

What stays with you is every decision. The AI never makes the call, never promises anything and never sends an email on its own. It prepares; you decide. That is the whole point of a simple routine.

A note on data and security

Phone calls often carry confidential details — health information, financial figures, client names. A recording or transcript of such a call has no place in a public consumer chatbot. Use a local model or a zero-retention enterprise service, and keep the notes in the client file where they belong. Where recording is not appropriate, plain notes in your own words work just as well.

The outcome

The phone still rings all day. But instead of a trail of sticky notes and half-remembered promises, you end each day with a short list of answered follow-ups and a client file that is actually up to date. Clients notice: they get their call back, their question answered, their message returned — with care, and without anything falling through the cracks.

Explanations Your Clients Actually Understand: An AI Routine for Plain-Language Advice

Clients Correspondence Languages

There is a moment in almost every client conversation where you can see it happen: you explain something you understand deeply, and the client's eyes glaze over. A notary describes a purchase-contract clause, a fiduciary explains a tax ruling, a doctor walks through a lab result — and the person across from you nods politely while understanding almost none of it.

The trouble is rarely the client. It is the distance between what you know and what they need to know. The good news is that closing that distance is a skill, not a talent — and it is one a calm AI routine can help you practise, one explanation at a time.

Why your expert language gets in the way

When you work with something every day, its language becomes invisible to you. Terms that feel precise and efficient — "restriction of the right to alienate", "deferred tax liability", "paroxysmal" — are simply noise to the person hearing them once. This is the classic curse of knowledge, and it has real consequences:

  • Clients do not act. A client who does not understand an explanation does not follow the advice in it, however sound that advice is.
  • Clients come back with the same question. An unclear explanation generates a second phone call and a third email, each one eating into your week.
  • Clients lose trust. People do not confuse clarity with incompetence; they confuse confusion with it. When they cannot follow you, they quietly wonder whether you can.

What plain language actually means

Plain language is not dumbing down, and it is not stripping out the facts. It is saying the same true thing in a way the reader can follow on the first pass. The difference is usually a few small habits:

  • One idea per sentence. Long sentences with three clauses are the main reason people reread a paragraph and still miss the point.
  • Short words over long ones. "Use" instead of "utilise", "end" instead of "termination", "about" instead of "approximately".
  • Concrete examples. An abstract rule becomes clear the moment you attach a number or a name to it.
  • A structure the eye can follow. A short heading, a few clear paragraphs and a short list beat a wall of text every time.

A calm AI routine for explaining clearly

You do not need to become a copywriter. You write your explanation the way you always would, and let the AI do the slow work of making it readable. In three unhurried steps:

Step 1 — Write the raw version

Put your explanation down exactly as you would say it. Do not try to simplify while you write; that is what the second step is for. The goal here is to capture the facts and the reasoning, nothing more.

Step 2 — Hand it to the AI with the audience

Tell the AI who is reading and what they need to leave with:

Here is my explanation for a client: [your raw text]. Rewrite it in plain language for a Swiss [notary client / fiduciary client / patient / small-office client] with no legal or medical background. Keep every fact, number and deadline exactly as it is. Use short sentences, one idea each, and replace jargon with everyday words. Structure it with a short heading and a few short paragraphs. Do not add advice I did not give.

Step 3 — Review for accuracy, not style

Read the result once, looking for one thing only: has any fact changed? Numbers, dates, obligations and warnings must stay identical. The AI is very good at simplifying; your job is to make sure the simplification did not simplify the truth.

A second prompt: the follow-up question

The best test of an explanation is not how it reads, but what the client asks next. Before you send it, ask the AI to play the client for a moment:

Read this explanation the way a client with no specialist background would: [your plain-language draft]. What is the first question a client would ask after reading it? Is there any sentence that is still confusing or could be read two ways? List up to three improvements that would make it clearer, and rewrite only those sentences.

One honest caveat

Plain language must never change the meaning. For legal, tax and medical explanations, the simplified version has to say exactly what the careful version says — the clarity is in the words, not in leaving things out. You remain responsible for every fact, and the AI is there to help you say it better, not to say less.

The outcome

After a few weeks you will notice the pattern: fewer second calls asking the same question, more clients who actually do what you advised, and a reputation for being the person who explains things clearly. That is the quiet, compounding payoff of a small routine — and it costs you one draft, one prompt and one careful read-through.

PPT Master for Client Proposals: From Documents to Editable Slides

DocumentsMarketingProductivity

Turning a project brief, report or service description into a client presentation can eat up an afternoon. PPT Master is an open-source workflow that asks an AI assistant to organise the argument and build an editable PowerPoint deck. It is promising for small firms that present their work often, but it is not a one-click website or a finished substitute for your judgement.

What PPT Master actually does

You give it source material such as a PDF, Word document, notes or a topic. An AI assistant works through a guided process, shapes a story for the slides, then exports a PowerPoint file. The result can contain editable text, shapes, charts and tables rather than screenshots of slides. You can also ask it to use an existing presentation as a template or fill a deck you already have.

The project is a workflow that runs inside an AI tool able to read and write files and run commands. It is not a standalone presentation app: you need to install the project and work with an agent-style assistant. That extra setup matters. If you only make one short deck a year, PowerPoint or Keynote may be simpler. PPT Master on GitHub.

Where a small business could use it

It may help when the same information needs to be presented clearly in different settings: a freelancer introducing a service, a consultant explaining a proposal, a training provider turning course notes into slides, or a small team summarising a project for a client. Starting from material you already trust can save the blank-page step and give you a first structure to improve.

For a client proposal, ask for a short deck with the problem, suggested approach, milestones and next steps. Give it your approved service description and scope, then compare every slide with those originals. If you already have a branded PowerPoint, the project describes workflows for reusing its design; still check fonts, spacing and logo placement before sending it.

  • Useful starting points: reports, service descriptions, workshop notes and approved proposal text.
  • Good first test: a short internal deck, not a high-stakes presentation going straight to a client.
  • Keep the original source files beside the exported deck so a reviewer can check the claims.

Editable does not mean ready to send

A generated deck can be a faster “first draft,” not a quality guarantee. The assistant may shorten a caveat, miss the point of a chart, or make a neat-looking slide from a weak argument. Check names, dates, figures, promises, prices and references against your source documents. For regulated or professional advice, have the responsible person review the content before it leaves the office.

Open the exported file in the presentation software your client will use. Inspect every slide at full size, including charts and tables, and check that the story still makes sense without the source document beside it. Native editable elements make corrections easier; they do not prove that the information is correct. Treat any suggested image or factual addition as something to verify.

Setup, cost and privacy

The project is free and open source. Its getting-started guide calls for Python 3.10 or newer, the project dependencies, and an AI tool that can follow the workflow. You also need an AI model. There is no model bundled with the project, so usage may cost money through the provider you choose. This is a more involved start than uploading a file to a presentation website.

The files and slide-building work run on your computer, but the AI assistant may send prompts or source content to its model provider. Local file storage alone does not make a workflow private. Before testing with client material, check your AI provider settings and terms, follow your firm’s confidentiality rules, and use dummy or redacted documents until you are confident. PPT Master is worth a small trial if editable client decks are a recurring task; if not, a familiar presentation app and a reusable template may be the more sensible routine.

Preparing Your Tax Return: An AI Routine for Self-employed and SMEs

Finance Documents Planning

A self-employed carpenter in Winterthur keeps his receipts in a shoebox and his invoices in a folder labelled "to sort". Every spring the same feeling arrives: the tax return is due, the documents are everywhere, and it all has to be right — because the tax office and the fiduciary are waiting.

Preparing the annual tax return is rarely difficult in the legal sense. It is difficult because it is scattered. Receipts sit in a drawer, bank statements live in the e-banking portal, and a dozen small decisions — private or business, deductible or not — pile up until the deadline forces them all at once.

The good news: this is exactly the kind of repetitive, document-heavy work an AI routine handles well. Not to do your taxes for you, but to gather, sort and draft — while every final decision stays with you.

Why the tax return feels so heavy

Ask any self-employed person or small office why they dread the annual return, and the answers are the same:

  • Documents everywhere: receipts in a shoebox, invoices in the inbox, statements in three different portals.
  • Private versus business: every single expense needs a decision, and the decisions quietly pile up over twelve months.
  • The fear of mistakes: one wrong number can trigger a query from the tax office, a correction, or a delayed assessment.

The result is a task that gets postponed until it has to be finished in one stressful weekend.

A once-a-year routine

Instead of one big mountain, break the return into three quiet steps. Each one takes a little time, and each one can be supported by AI.

Step 1 — Collect everything into one list

Start with a single checklist. Give the AI the documents you know you need — or simply your profession and the year — and let it draft the list you should collect. Then work through it in peace.

I am preparing my 2025 tax return as a self-employed [profession]. Draft a checklist of the documents and figures I need: income, expenses, insurance, pension, debt interest, and anything else typical for my situation. Keep it in plain language, one item per line.

Step 2 — Separate private from business

Once the documents are together, the real work begins: deciding what counts as business and what is private. The AI can draft the first split for you. You review and correct.

Here is a list of my expenses for the year. Sort each one into three groups: clearly business, clearly private, and unclear. For the unclear ones, write one sentence on why they are uncertain and what information would settle it. Do not invent figures — work only with what I give you.

Step 3 — Draft the summary and the answers

Most returns need a short cover note for the fiduciary or the tax office, and answers to a few standard questions. Let the AI draft both from the sorted material, then adjust the wording and check the numbers yourself.

What AI does well — and what stays with you

  • Sorting and summarising: turning a messy pile of items into a clear, ordered list.
  • Drafting the cover note: a short, neutral explanation of what is in the return and what you assumed.
  • Spotting gaps: flagging the documents that seem to be missing before the tax office does.

What stays with you is the judgement: every private-or-business call, every figure, and the final responsibility. The AI prepares; you decide.

A note on data and security

Tax documents are sensitive. Client names, social security numbers, income figures and account details have no place in a public consumer chatbot. Use an approved setup — a local model or a zero-retention enterprise service — or anonymise the data first and add the real details back into the final documents yourself.

The outcome

Three or four quiet hours, spread over a week, are usually enough to turn the annual tax return from a dreaded pile into a tidy, finished submission. The checklist exists, the documents are sorted, the summary is drafted — and you send it off with a clear head instead of a knot in your stomach.

Filing Your Quarterly VAT: An AI Routine for Self-employed and SMEs

Compliance Finance Planning

Four times a year, the same quiet ritual arrives for every Swiss business that is registered for VAT: the quarterly statement. The turnover has to be right, the input tax has to match the receipts, and the form has to go to the FTA on time. It is rarely difficult — it simply has to be correct, and it always seems to land on a week when you had other plans.

For a notary, a fiduciary, a doctor's practice or a small office, the VAT return is one of those tasks that is small on paper and heavy in reality. It sits in the background for weeks, then demands a concentrated evening of gathering figures and double-checking numbers.

Why the quarterly VAT statement feels heavy

The work itself is not the problem. It is everything around it:

  • Figures scattered everywhere. Turnover lives in your invoicing tool, input VAT lives in a pile of receipts, and the two are never in the same place.
  • Matching receipts to categories. Which rate applies to this expense? Was this purchase for the business or for yourself?
  • The deadline in the background. The form is due shortly after the end of the quarter, and it quietly adds pressure to an already full week.

The result is familiar: a task you do four times a year, each time as if it were the first, and each time slightly later than you meant to.

A simple routine in three steps

You do not need new software or a complicated accounting setup. You need one quiet hour per quarter and a small, repeatable routine.

Step 1 — Gather the quarter's figures into one list

Export your turnover from your invoicing or bookkeeping tool, and put your receipts in one place — a folder, a scan, a simple list. You are not sorting yet; you are only collecting, so nothing is missing later.

Step 2 — Let the AI sort and match

Hand the AI the raw list and ask it to do the mechanical part: group the amounts, match receipts to the right rate, and flag anything unclear. A prompt like this does the heavy lifting:

I am a small Swiss business preparing my quarterly VAT return. Below is my turnover for the quarter and a list of expenses. Please sort the expenses into the correct Swiss VAT categories (standard rate, reduced rate, special rate, exempt, or not deductible), sum the amounts by category, and list any item where the rate or the treatment is unclear so I can check it myself. Do not invent figures — leave a blank where something is missing. Turnover: [paste]. Expenses: [paste].

Step 3 — Review and submit in one sitting

Go through the sorted list once, check the flagged items, transfer the numbers into the form, and submit. Because the AI already did the sorting and the arithmetic, this final pass is quick and careful instead of a late-night scramble.

A second prompt for the tricky items

Some expenses are genuinely unclear — a partly private phone, a mixed-use car, a purchase you made before registering. For those, ask the AI to lay out the options without deciding for you:

Here are a few expenses I am unsure about for my Swiss VAT return: [paste]. For each one, explain in plain language which Swiss VAT treatment could apply and what information I would need to decide. Do not choose for me — just clarify the options so I can decide with care.

What the AI does well — and what stays with you

  • Sorting and grouping: the same receipts, always matched to the right category, without the fatigue of the tenth item.
  • Arithmetic: sums and subtotals are done for you, so the transfer errors disappear.
  • Flagging the unclear: the AI points to exactly the items you should look at, instead of you re-checking everything.

What stays with you is the judgement: which treatment is actually correct, whether a purchase was business or private, and the final responsibility for what is submitted. The AI is a careful assistant, never the signatory.

A note on data and privacy

A VAT return is full of financial figures, so treat it like any other sensitive business data. Do not paste client names or account numbers into a public chatbot. Use a local model or a zero-retention service, or anonymise the list first and add the names back yourself. The Swiss Data Protection Act applies here too.

The outcome

One quiet hour per quarter replaces the late-night scramble. The return is filed on time, the figures are right, and the task stops looming over the whole month. You keep four evenings a year — and a little more peace of mind.

Replies That Sound Like You: An AI Routine for Your Recurring Emails

Email Templates Clients

A notary in Zurich writes the same three sentences about the next appointment a dozen times a week. A dentist in Geneva confirms, reschedules and sends the same payment details every day. A fiduciary in Bern answers "please find attached" so often it has become muscle memory. None of it is difficult — it simply never stops, and every reply starts from a blank page.

These recurring emails are the quiet background hum of a small practice. They are not billable, not strategic and rarely remembered — but they still have to be written well, because they are the voice your clients actually hear most often.

Why recurring emails quietly drain you

The cost is not one big problem. It is a hundred tiny ones, repeated every single day:

  • Starting from scratch. You rewrite the same appointment confirmation from memory, slightly differently each time.
  • An uneven tone. The reply you write at seven in the morning sounds different from the one you write at five in the afternoon, tired, after a long day.
  • Small errors. By the third repetition of the day the typos creep in, the wrong address gets pasted, the attachment is forgotten.

The result is familiar: replies that sound rushed, vary from day to day, and quietly steal the time you meant to spend on real work.

A simple routine in three steps

You do not need new software or a complicated system. You need one unhurried hour to build a small library of replies that already sound like you.

Step 1 — Collect your recurring emails

For one week, notice which emails you write more than once: appointment confirmations, requests for missing documents, payment details, directions to the office, the short "thank you", the gentle reminder. Write the list down. Most practices have between five and fifteen of these.

Step 2 — Let the AI draft templates in your voice

Hand the AI a few of your own real replies — with names and sensitive details removed — and ask it to turn them into reusable templates that match your tone. A prompt like this does the heavy lifting:

I run a small practice in Switzerland. Below are a few real emails I have written to clients. Please draft reusable templates in my tone for the messages I write most often: an appointment confirmation, a request for missing documents, a note with the payment details, and a short thank-you. Keep the wording natural and friendly, leave placeholders like [name], [date] and [amount] where something changes, and do not add any marketing phrases I did not use. Emails: [paste your own, names removed].

Step 3 — Save, review, reuse

Store the finished templates where you can reach them in one click — in your email program's template or signature feature, in a simple notes file, or in a small document. When a recurring email comes up, open the template, fill in the one or two lines that change, read it once and send.

A second prompt for the tricky ones

Some recurring messages need a little more care — a rescheduling note, a small price change, a delay. For those, ask the AI to keep the tone warm and to say no pressure:

Draft a short, friendly message to a client to reschedule next week's appointment. Tone: warm, no urgency. Mention that a new time can be found together and that there is no rush. Leave a placeholder for the proposed new date.

What the AI does well — and what stays with you

  • Drafting the structure: the same complete, friendly skeleton for every message, so nothing is forgotten.
  • Matching your voice: the AI learns your wording from your own examples, so replies stop sounding generic.
  • Keeping it consistent: every client gets the same professional tone, no matter when you write.

What stays with you is the human part: the personal touch, the judgement about what a particular client needs to hear, and the final approval before anything is sent.

A note on data and privacy

Templates are usually harmless — a standard appointment confirmation carries no personal data. But the moment a reply contains a client's name, health details or financial figures, do not paste it into a public chatbot. Use a local model or a zero-retention service, or anonymise the message first and add the real names back yourself. The Swiss Data Protection Act applies to client data even in something as small as an email.

The outcome

  • The missed deadline. A filing date, a transitional period, a new fee schedule. Missing it is rarely fatal, but it is always avoidable.
  • The outdated advice. You answer a client from memory, and the rule changed six months ago.
  • The background anxiety. A low, constant hum of "what have I missed?" that follows you home.
  • The wasted hour. Re-reading a forty-page circular in full when only two pages touch your practice.

A calm routine to stay current

You do not need to read everything. You need a small system that collects, filters and condenses — and lets you decide in one sitting. Here is a routine you can run once a month, in a single quiet hour.

Step 1 — Collect your sources in one place

Make a short list of the places that actually matter to your practice: the official newsletters, your professional association, the tax administration, a legal database, one or two specialist publications. Here is the latest circular from the tax administration. Summarise it for a fiduciary in Switzerland. Step 3 — Keep a one-page register

For every item that actually matters, write one line in a running document: the date, the source, what changed, the deadline, and what you decided to do. Over time this register becomes your own map of the rules that govern your practice — searchable, calm, always up to date.

Step 4 — Book the review hour

Treat every summary as a first draft: useful, fast, and always to be checked.

And when a client asks about a recent change, you answer from your register, not from memory or worry. Staying current stops being a burden you carry around and becomes a small, reliable system — one hour a month, and the confidence that nothing important is slipping past.

AI agents — tools that don't just answer questions, but act on their own: reading files, sending emails, running tasks — are arriving fast in small Swiss offices. The benefits are real. So are the risks, and most people don't yet understand them.

Why this matters for your business

An agent that can read your emails, files or invoices is useful precisely because it can act. But that same access is what makes a bad add-on dangerous.
