The good news: you don't need to be a security expert to cut the risk sharply. A few habits, plus one or two tools, cover most of it.

Check before you install

Before adding any new skill or add-on, ask three questions:

  • Who made it? Prefer tools from a well-known maker with an active community over anonymous one-file add-ons.
  • What does it touch? A skill that only tidies text is very different from one that asks for your inbox or your bank files.
  • Can it be checked? Tools such as NVIDIA's SkillSpector can look at a skill and flag hidden instructions, data leaks and sneaky backdoors before you install it.

Keep agents in a safe box

When an agent needs real access, put a boundary around it. A “sandbox” — a sealed-off area it can work in — lets the agent do its job in a space you can simply delete afterwards. Stronger tools like OpenShell add another layer: they enforce rules deep in the system, so the agent can only read the files, use the logins and reach the websites you explicitly allow.

For most Swiss SMEs, the everyday version is even simpler: keep agents on a separate account, never hand over your main password, and check anything sensitive before it goes out.

A three-step habit

  1. Check any new skill before you install it.
  2. Run agents you're unsure about in a sandbox, not on your main machine.
  3. Keep client data out of tools you haven't checked.

That's it. You don't need to ban AI. You just need the same care you already apply to any tool that handles client data.

SkillSpector: A Free Scanner That Checks AI Add-Ons Before You Install Them

SecurityData protectionAI Agents

Your AI assistant learns new tricks through add-ons: ready-made instruction packages that teach it to draft offers, read files or answer in your tone. Handy — and a bit like installing software from a stranger. A free scanner from NVIDIA now looks inside such add-ons before you install them.

What a “skill” actually is

Tools like Claude Code, Codex or Gemini CLI load small packages called skills. A skill is usually a text file with instructions, sometimes with small scripts attached. It shows your AI how to handle a task — and it typically runs with access to whatever the assistant can see: files, text you paste, sometimes the network.

Most skills come from public marketplaces and repositories. Many are genuinely useful and harmless. But an add-on that can read what your AI reads is an add-on worth a second look.

The uncomfortable numbers

SkillSpector was built on a research study that examined 42,447 skills from major marketplaces. The result: 26.1 percent contained at least one security flaw, and 5.2 percent showed signs of likely malicious intent. Skills that include executable scripts were more than twice as likely to be problematic.

Two dangers matter most for an office:

  • Hidden instructions: a skill can contain orders your AI follows without showing you — for example “ignore the previous rules”, or directions tucked away in comments.
  • Quiet data leaks: a skill can send content outward — text from your files, saved passwords, file paths — to an address you never chose.

If your assistant can open client documents, a badly behaved add-on can too.

What the scanner does

SkillSpector, released as open source (Apache 2.0) by NVIDIA, examines a skill before installation. You point it at a link, a folder or a zip file, and it works in two passes:

  • First pass: fast static checks against 64 known vulnerability patterns in 16 categories — hidden instructions, data leaks, supply-chain tricks, excessive permissions — plus a live check of the skill’s building blocks against a public database of known weak spots.
  • Second pass (optional): an AI model reads the flagged passages in context and sorts out false alarms. This pass can even run against a local model such as Ollama, so the scan itself sends nothing to a cloud.

The result is a risk score from 0 to 100, a severity label and a report that points to the exact line behind every finding — so whoever looks after your IT can judge, not just trust a number.

What this means for a Swiss small business

You don’t have to run the scanner yourself to take the lesson seriously. Under the revised Swiss data protection law, you remain responsible for client data that your tools touch — a leak through a “helpful” add-on is still your leak. A few habits cover most of the risk:

  1. Install AI add-ons only from sources you can name.
  2. Ask what an add-on is allowed to read before it comes near client files.
  3. Have new add-ons checked first — with SkillSpector, or by whoever looks after your IT.
  4. Keep client data away from tools nobody has checked.

Honest limits: a scan is a snapshot, not a guarantee — it analyses code, not behaviour at runtime, and it cannot read text hidden in images. And the tool is built for agent skills specifically; if you never install such add-ons, the habit matters more than the tool. The convenience of one-click AI extensions is real. So is the responsibility that comes with it.

Write It Down Once: An AI Routine for Your Standard Office Processes

WorkflowDocumentsQuality

The most important document in a small office is usually the one nobody ever wrote down: how things are actually done. Who opens the mail, how a new client is taken on, how the monthly billing runs, where the backups live, what happens on the first of the month. It all lives in one head — yours.

That works fine, until it does not. The day you are ill, or finally on holiday, or you bring in a helper and have to explain the same task for the tenth time. Then the office quietly depends on a single person who cannot be in two places at once.

Why "just ask me" stops working

Every small practice starts this way, and there is nothing wrong with it. But over the years the same costs start to show:

  • A single point of failure. If only you know how the billing or the client intake runs, nothing moves while you are away.
  • Training takes forever. Explaining a task live, each time slightly differently, is slow for both sides.
  • Inconsistency. What you explain on Monday may differ from what you explain on Thursday.
  • Holidays feel risky. You do not really switch off, because half of your attention stays at the office.

A calm routine to write it down

You do not need to document everything at once. You need one short routine, repeated once a week, until the most important processes are on paper.

Step 1 — Collect what you actually do

For one week, keep a simple list. Every time you finish a recurring task — sending the quarterly VAT, onboarding a new client, preparing a file — write down one line: what it is and roughly how long it takes. At the end of the week you have the raw material for your process notes.

Step 2 — Let the AI turn each task into steps

Take one task and give the AI everything you know about it, in plain words. Ask for a first draft of a step-by-step instruction:

Here is how I take on a new client: I receive the enquiry by email, check the conflict list, send a short reply with a link to book a call, then prepare an intake note before the meeting. Turn this into a clear step-by-step instruction for someone who has never done it. Use short numbered steps, plain language, and mark anything that is a legal or confidentiality requirement as "must". Leave out any fluff.

Step 3 — Add the details only you know

The AI drafts the skeleton, but the soul of a process note is the small things only you know: where the template lives, which login to use, who to call when something is unclear, and the one exception to the rule. Add these as notes after each step.

Step 4 — Test it on a fresh pair of eyes

Give the draft to someone who does not know the task — a colleague, a family member, or simply yourself after a week away. Wherever they stop and ask, the note has a gap. Fill it in.

What belongs in a good process note

A useful process note is short and answers five questions. If it does, you can hand it to anyone with confidence:

  • The trigger. What starts the task — a client email, the first of the month, an invoice arriving?
  • The steps. In the order they happen, each one small enough to follow.
  • The tools. Which folder, template, software or login is involved.
  • The exception. What to do when the standard path does not fit.
  • The finish line. What "done" looks like, so the task does not drift on.

Here is a second prompt, for when you already have a draft and want it checked:

Here is my process note for sending payment reminders. Check it for gaps: is any step unclear, is anything missing that a newcomer would not know, and are there any assumptions I have not written down? Ask me the questions one by one, and I will answer, then update the note.

What AI cannot do for you

The AI can draft and tidy, but it does not know your office. It will not notice that the backup runs on the old laptop in the cupboard, or that the notary prefers a call to an email. The knowledge is yours; the AI just helps you get it out of your head and into a form others can follow. And as always: keep client names, patient details and confidential figures out of public models. Write the process in general terms, or use a local model.

The outcome

After a few weeks you have a small folder of process notes — the way your office actually runs, written down once and easy to update. The first time you take a holiday without checking your email, or hand a task to someone else and watch it get done without you, you will feel the difference. The office stops living in your head and starts living on paper, where it can be shared, improved and trusted. That is the quiet kind of progress that pays off for years.

AI and the Swiss Data Protection Act: What Self-employed and SMEs Must Know

Privacy Compliance Workflow

Swiss self-employed professionals and SMEs are already using AI every day: to draft emails, summarize meetings, translate offers, clean up notes, or turn a rough outline into a first version of a contract or report. The practical question is no longer whether AI exists in your office. The real question is whether you are using it in a way that respects your clients, your staff, and Swiss law.

The good news is simple: the Swiss Data Protection Act does not ban AI. But it does follow your data into the tool. If personal data goes into an AI workflow, the usual data-protection duties still apply. The FDPIC has stated clearly that the Federal Data Protection Act, in force since 1 September 2023, applies directly to AI-supported data processing. So the goal is not panic and it is not blind adoption. The goal is a explainable workflow.

The answer: AI is allowed, but the rules still travel with the data

That point matters because many business owners still think in extremes. Either AI is treated as magic software that somehow sits outside normal compliance, or it is treated as a forbidden zone that should never touch real work. Both views are unhelpful. The law is technology-neutral. If you process personal data with a spreadsheet, a CRM, a transcription tool, or a language model, the central questions remain familiar: why are you processing the data, what data do you really need, who receives it, how long is it kept, and what safeguards are in place?

For a small Swiss business, that means you do not need a 40-page policy before testing AI. But you do need the habit of asking a few disciplined questions before you paste client emails, CVs, patient notes, payroll data, or meeting transcripts into a tool. Practical AI becomes much less stressful once you stop asking “Is AI legal?” and start asking “Is this specific workflow proportionate, transparent, and controlled?”

Start with one question: is there personal data in the prompt?

This is the simplest filter and often the most useful one. Personal data is not only a passport number or a medical diagnosis. In everyday office life, it also includes names, business email addresses, phone numbers, salary information, evaluation notes, application documents, customer complaints, call transcripts, and any text that points to an identifiable person.

A company name on its own is not always the problem. But real business files almost never contain only company names. A consulting brief includes a contact person. An offer request includes a mobile number. An HR spreadsheet includes performance comments. A doctor’s note includes health information. A legal draft may include identities, family relations, or financial details. Once identifiable people are in the workflow, the Data Protection Act is relevant.

That does not mean you must stop. It means you should classify the material before you use AI. A prompt that says “write me five headlines for a LinkedIn post about succession planning” is very different from a prompt that uploads a real client dossier. Treating both actions as equally risky is what creates confusion and leads teams either to over-share or to freeze unnecessarily.

A practical three-zone model for daily work

One simple way to make better decisions is to sort AI use cases into three zones:

  • Low-risk use: no personal data, or only public and non-sensitive material. Examples: drafting marketing copy, translating your own generic notes, summarizing a public regulation, or turning bullet points into a standard agenda. Standard tools are often enough here.
  • Medium-risk use: limited personal data with low consequence, especially after minimization. Examples: drafting a client reply after replacing names with roles, summarizing an internal meeting with initials instead of full names, or turning discovery notes into an offer outline. Here, minimization and human review matter a lot, and business-grade settings are usually preferable.
  • High-risk use: sensitive or consequential data. Examples: patient records, legal files, HR evaluations, payroll exports, ID scans, disciplinary notes, social situations, or automated scoring of applicants, employees, or customers. These cases deserve approved enterprise setups, strong contractual clarity, or local processing, and sometimes a formal risk assessment.

This three-zone model is not a legal formula. It is a management habit. It helps a team avoid the two classic errors: feeding too much data into convenient consumer tools, or blocking harmless AI tasks that could save time with almost no privacy downside.

Five checks before you use any AI tool

  1. Define the purpose in one sentence. If the only answer is “because it is faster,” you are not finished yet. A better answer sounds like this: “We use AI to turn handwritten meeting notes into a first draft summary that is reviewed by the project lead before it is shared.” A clear purpose makes it much easier to decide what data is actually necessary.
  2. Minimize the data before it leaves your hands. Remove names if roles are enough. Replace exact dates with months if precision is unnecessary. Leave out signatures, account numbers, attachments, and full histories unless they are essential for the task. In many office workflows, you keep most of the AI benefit even after stripping out the identifying details.
  3. Check the provider setup, not only the model quality. Public consumer tools, enterprise APIs, and local models are not the same thing. Look at whether your inputs are stored, whether they may be used for training, where the processing takes place, who can access the data, and what contractual protections exist if the data leaves Switzerland. Under Swiss rules, cross-border transfers depend on the destination and the safeguards in place, so this is not a minor detail.
  4. Keep transparency and human review in the loop. The FDPIC links transparency closely to the rights of individuals in automated processing. In practice, that means two very simple habits. First, if a person is chatting with a machine on your website or in your support flow, say so clearly. Second, if AI suggests something that materially affects a person — for example an applicant ranking, a customer decision, or a compliance flag — do not let the machine be the final word.
  5. Document who may use which tool for which data. You do not need an enterprise governance platform to be serious. A shared page with approved tools, allowed data types, and one responsible contact person is already far better than a culture of secret copy-paste from private accounts. Small businesses get into trouble less because of advanced AI and more because nobody wrote down the rules.
“The safest AI workflow is usually not the most sophisticated one. It is the one your team can explain, repeat, and audit six months later.”

What to avoid if you want fewer surprises

Most privacy problems around AI do not come from a dramatic security breach. They come from casual habits. A useful rule of thumb is this: if you would feel uncomfortable explaining the workflow to a client, an employee, or a regulator in one paragraph, the setup is probably too loose.

  • Avoid dumping full inboxes or CRM exports into a generic chat window when you do not know the retention rules or training settings.
  • Avoid uploading sensitive files just because the work is internal. Internal does not automatically mean low risk.
  • Avoid treating AI output as a final record. Summaries, translations, and extracted action items still need a human check.
  • Avoid shadow AI in personal accounts. Convenience is a poor substitute for a documented company process.
  • Avoid hiding automation from people who interact with it directly. If the first response is generated by a machine, clear labeling is the safer default.

None of this is anti-AI. It is simply the difference between deliberate use and unplanned leakage.

When zero-retention or local AI makes sense

If you only need help with generic writing, broad brainstorming, or public information, standard cloud tools may be perfectly adequate. But once you regularly handle confidential client material, HR documents, medical notes, legal drafts, or internal knowledge bases, a stronger setup becomes worthwhile.

A zero-retention or no-training business setup means the provider processes the request but does not keep the content for model training and usually offers clearer contractual terms around security and data handling. For many SMEs, this is the practical middle ground: you keep the convenience of cloud AI without casually feeding your firm’s know-how back into a public system.

Local AI means the model runs on your own machine or inside infrastructure you control. It usually needs more setup and may not match the biggest cloud models on every task. But it gives you far better control over where sensitive data lives. For doctors, fiduciaries, law firms, and any business handling recurring confidential documents, that control often matters more than having the fanciest model on the market.

The right question is not “local or cloud?” in the abstract. It is “which tasks justify which setup?” Many firms do well with a mixed model: ordinary drafting in a controlled cloud environment, and highly sensitive work only in local or specially approved systems.

Do you need a DPIA or extra review?

Under Swiss rules, high-risk processing can require a data protection impact assessment. The FDPIC highlights this especially where processing is likely to create a high risk to personality or fundamental rights, particularly when new technologies are involved. That does not mean every new AI experiment needs a formal project. It does mean you should slow down when the impact on people becomes more serious.

Practical warning signs include large-scale use of sensitive data, automated decisions about applicants or employees, systematic monitoring, broad profiling, or the combination of multiple data sources to evaluate people. If one of those signs is present, do not roll out the workflow casually. Document the intended use, the risks, the safeguards, and whether you need specialist advice before going further.

Many everyday AI tasks will never cross that threshold. Drafting a sanitized email, turning your own rough notes into clearer prose, or summarizing a non-sensitive project meeting is not the same as building an AI system that ranks job candidates or predicts patient risk.

A simple AI privacy policy for a Swiss small business

If you want something practical that your team can actually follow, start with five short rules:

  1. Public AI tools are for no personal data or minimized data only.
  2. Sensitive work goes only into approved business or local tools.
  3. Anything sent externally after AI drafting is reviewed by a human.
  4. If AI interacts directly with clients, applicants, or patients, it is labeled clearly and a human contact remains available.
  5. We keep a simple register of tools, purposes, data types, retention expectations, and cross-border questions.

That is not bureaucratic theatre. It is a small operating rule that reduces confusion, gives your staff confidence, and makes future tool choices easier. In many companies, the biggest privacy improvement is not a new vendor. It is moving from improvised individual behavior to a shared, repeatable standard.

Use AI with care, not casually

The Swiss Data Protection Act is not an obstacle to practical AI. It is a reminder that efficiency does not cancel responsibility. If you choose small, clear use cases, minimize data, stay transparent, and match the tool to the sensitivity of the work, AI can save real time without turning your business into a compliance experiment.

Start with one workflow. Write down the rules. Keep the human review. For most self-employed professionals and SMEs, that is enough to move from anxious guessing to responsible everyday use.

The Swiss QR-Bill Without Errors: An AI Routine for Your Invoices

Invoicing Finance Payments

Since June 2020, every invoice in Switzerland carries a QR-bill — the payment slip with the Swiss QR code that replaced the old orange and red slips. For a self-employed person or a small office, it is one of those tasks that should be trivial, yet quietly causes trouble: a wrong reference, a missing QR-IBAN, or a message line that breaks the machine reading.

The good news is that the QR-bill is not complicated once you know the few fields that matter. And the reassuring part: most of the fiddly assembly — checking the reference, lining up the fields, drafting the invoice text — is exactly what AI is good at.

Why the QR-bill still trips people up

The QR-bill looks simple, but small mistakes are common and they cost time more than anything. A bill that a scanner cannot read means a phone call from the client, a corrected invoice, and a delayed payment.

  • The QR-IBAN. The QR reference only works with a QR-IBAN. Mix a normal IBAN with a QR reference and the payment can be rejected.
  • The reference. The 27-digit QR reference has a check digit. One mistyped digit and the whole line fails.
  • The message lines. The unstructured message has strict rules about length and characters; get them wrong and the data no longer fits the code.
  • The layout. The payment part must sit at the bottom, with a receipt section, a separator line, and a QR code with enough quiet space around it.

What a QR-bill actually needs

Strip away the layout and the QR-bill is just a short list of fields. If these are right, the rest follows:

  • Account / Payable to: your IBAN (ideally a QR-IBAN), plus your name and address.
  • Reference: either the 27-digit QR reference or a structured creditor reference.
  • Amount and currency: CHF or EUR, written clearly.
  • Payable by: the client's name and address.
  • Additional information: the invoice number and a short message, in the right format.

An AI routine to build one

Step 1 — Keep a master block

Write down your own payment details once — IBAN, name, address, and your preferred reference style — in a short note you can reuse. This is the only part that never changes, and it is the part most likely to contain a typo if you retype it every time.

Step 2 — Let the AI assemble the fields

Give the AI your master block and the invoice details, and ask it to prepare the payment data in the right format:

You are helping a Swiss self-employed person prepare a QR-bill. My details: [name], [address], IBAN [QR-IBAN]. Invoice: number [n], amount [amount] CHF, client [name and address]. Please list the fields in the correct QR-bill format — account, reference, amount, currency, payable by, and the additional information line with the invoice number — and flag anything missing or inconsistent.

Step 3 — Proofread the reference

Read the reference digit by digit against your records before you save the invoice. This is the one field no machine can fix for you, and it is the one that sends a payment to the wrong place when it is wrong.

A second prompt: checking the bill

Before you send, let the AI check the finished invoice the way a careful colleague would:

Check this invoice for common Swiss QR-bill mistakes: is the QR reference consistent with the QR-IBAN, is the amount written correctly, are the message lines within the allowed length, and is the payment part at the bottom with a receipt section? List anything that would stop the bill from being scanned correctly.

The AI does not draw the QR code itself, and it should not. Generate the code with your invoicing software or your bank's online tool, then let the AI handle the words around it — the fields, the message, the proofread. Treat the AI as the careful colleague who checks the details, not as the printer.

One short master note, one prompt to assemble the fields, and one read-through of the reference. A QR-bill that used to take twenty careful minutes and still came back with errors becomes a two-minute routine — and the payments arrive on time because the bill is right the first time.

Why the client list drifts into disorder

The mess is rarely anyone's fault. It is the natural result of how a practice grows:

  • Duplicates: the same client is entered as "Müller GmbH", "Mueller GmbH" and "Müller AG", so three records share one history.
  • Outdated details: addresses, phone numbers and bank details change quietly, and the old version keeps being used for months.
  • Missing pieces: some contacts lack a postal code, others lack an email, and a few lack both.

The cost shows up in small, awkward ways: a letter returns as undeliverable, an invoice goes to the wrong address, or a client receives two reminders because two records were billed separately.

A simple routine in three passes

You don't need to clean the whole list in one heroic weekend. Three quiet passes, done once and then kept light, are enough.

Pass 1 — Merge the duplicates

Export your contacts as a plain list and let the AI group the entries that probably belong to the same person or company. It drafts the merge; you decide.

Here is an exported list of my clients and contacts. Group the entries that are clearly the same person or company — for example different spellings, old and new addresses, or a person and their company. For each group, show which record should be kept and which should be merged into it. Do not merge anything you are unsure about; put those in a separate list and explain why.

Pass 2 — Fill in the gaps

Next, the AI flags the records with missing or clearly outdated details and drafts what should be added — a missing postal code, a missing language preference, an old phone number.

Go through my contact list and flag every entry with missing or obviously outdated information: missing postal codes, missing email addresses, old phone numbers, incomplete company names. For each one, write what seems to be missing and, where the data allows, suggest the likely correct value. Never invent details — mark anything you cannot verify as "to confirm".

Pass 3 — Standardise the format

Finally, the AI brings the list into one consistent format: company names written the same way, addresses in the Swiss format, salutations and languages noted. This is the pass that makes future work easier.

What AI does well — and what stays with you

  • Spotting duplicates and near-duplicates: finding the "Müller/Mueller" pairs that a human eye skips over.
  • Drafting the corrections: proposing the right address, the right name, the right format.
  • Keeping the work small: a tidy list is easier to keep tidy, so each future pass gets shorter.

What stays with you is every decision. The AI never writes into your client database on its own; it prepares, you approve. That is the whole point of a simple routine.

A note on data and security

Your client list is sensitive — names, addresses, dates of birth, sometimes health or financial details. It has no place in a public consumer chatbot. Use an approved setup: a local model or a zero-retention enterprise service, or anonymise the data first and add the real details back yourself at the end.

The outcome

One quiet afternoon is usually enough to turn a drifted, duplicate-laden list into a clean, trustworthy address book. The next invoice goes to the right address, the next letter reaches the right person, and you stop discovering — too late — that two records were really one client all along.

The routine has three steps and fits into one quiet hour at the end of the month. The aim is not to account for every second, but to produce a correct, complete invoice without the usual friction.

Step 1 — Gather the month in one place

Let the AI bring the raw material together: the calendar entries, the notes, the emails about a mandate. You do not type anything; you paste or forward, and the AI merges it all into a single list of dated entries.

Why open items pile up

The open items themselves are not the problem. The problem is that they live in different places — the inbox, the notebook, a sticky note, your head — and because each one is small, it gets postponed. Individually they cost almost nothing. Together they become a permanent background hum.

  • They live in different places: one sits in the inbox, one on a slip of paper, one only in your memory.
  • They are never urgent — until they are: the "small" task that suddenly blocks a client mandate.
  • They follow you home: the open loop that keeps you half-thinking about work in the evening.

The 20-minute weekly review

The routine has three steps and fits into the last twenty minutes of the week — a Friday afternoon is a good place for it. The point is not to do everything, but to see everything and decide.

Step 1: Collect everything onto one list

Gather the open items from wherever they live: the inbox, the notes, the half-written drafts, the "next week" pile. Let the AI merge them into a single list of Pendenzen.

Here are my open items from this week — emails, notes and drafts below. Merge them into one list. For each item, give a short title, say who it is for, and mark whether it is a reply, a decision or a task. Leave out duplicates. Do not invent anything.

Not everything on the list deserves your attention. Let the AI sort the items by consequence: what happens if this waits another week? Then mark each one — do now, delegate, schedule, or drop.

Step 3: Draft the replies and schedule the rest

For the items that need a reply, let the AI draft it — factual, no pressure. For the items that need time, put them on the calendar. The goal is that nothing stays "somewhere at the back of your mind".

Draft a short, friendly reply for these three items. Tone: factual, no urgency. Also suggest a date next week for the two tasks that need time.

Why this works — and what stays human

The review works because it is small and repeatable. You are not reorganising your whole office; you are giving twenty minutes to a single habit. Over a few weeks the open items stop accumulating, because they are caught early instead of carried in your head.

What stays human is the decision about what matters. The AI never sets your priorities; it only makes the list visible and does the typing. You decide who needs an answer today, which task can wait, and which one can be dropped entirely.

The list often contains client names and matters, so the usual rules apply. Use a business-grade tool rather than a private consumer account, check whether the provider stores your input or trains on it, and anonymise first if you are unsure — replace names with placeholders, work out the structure, and add the real details afterwards.

Start this Friday. Twenty minutes, one list. The first week you will simply see everything that has been floating around. From the second week on, less and less will pile up — because you are no longer holding it all in your head.

What AI Actually Costs: A Transparent Guide for Swiss Businesses

Costs Finance Planning

"What does it actually cost?" — that is the first question whenever AI comes up at work. Fair enough: nobody wants to pay for tools they do not need, and nobody wants to be pushed into a subscription that eats a little more each month. The good news up front: AI is cheaper than most people think — if you look carefully instead of chasing the next headline.

This guide is honest and free of sales pressure. You get the real price bands, the hidden costs, and a clear way to decide what is worth it for your office — whether you run a notary's practice, a fiduciary, a doctor's surgery or a small office.

The three price bands, simply put

Almost every AI tool sits in one of three bands. That is all you need to orient yourself.

  • Free: ChatGPT, Claude and others offer free tiers. They are enough for trying things out and for occasional tasks — a draft letter, a summary, a list of ideas. You give up comfort in return: less speed, smaller limits, and your input may be used for training.
  • Around 20 to 30 francs a month: the individual plans such as ChatGPT Plus or Claude Pro. For most self-employed people this is the point where the work gets noticeably lighter: better models, longer texts, more reliable operation. A single subscription of this kind is almost always enough.
  • From around 25 francs per person per month: team and business tiers. These only pay off once several people work together and you want shared templates, permissions and — important in Switzerland — settings that keep your data out of training.

The figures are ballpark values and can change. What matters is not the franc amount but whether the tool gives you time back.

What you actually pay — and what you do not

The subscription price is only part of the bill. If you calculate honestly, three things belong in it:

  • The subscription: 0 to about 30 francs a month for a single seat.
  • Your time: setting up the first templates and task lists costs a few quiet hours. That is not an expense but an investment that pays for itself within a few weeks.
  • The data decision: if you work with client or patient data, a plan with privacy settings or a local model is the safer choice — a few francs more, but far less worry.

Local or cloud: an honest comparison

One question keeps coming up: is a local model on your own computer worth it? The answer depends on your data.

Local models cost nothing per month but need a decent computer and a little setup time. They are the right choice when confidential data must not leave the house. Cloud plans are more convenient and more capable, but they ask for trust in the provider. Both are legitimate — what matters is that you make the choice deliberately, not out of habit.

Write me an honest comparison for my office: an individual plan with ChatGPT or Claude against a local model. List monthly costs, setup effort and data protection. I run a fiduciary with one person and work with client data.

The hidden costs — and how to keep them small

AI rarely becomes expensive through the subscription, but through three detours:

  • Too many tools: whoever signs up for five subscriptions pays five times and ends up using two. Start with one tool and stick with it until you really know what you need.
  • Unused features: the pricier tiers add image generation, data analysis and more — useful, but often unnecessary in daily office work. Only pay for what you use every week.
  • No cancellation rhythm: subscriptions quietly keep running. A diary date every six months to check what you actually use keeps the costs small.
List my current AI tools and subscriptions and tell me which one I could drop. For each, note what I actually use it for, and whether a single tool could cover several of those tasks.

A clear way to decide

You do not have to rush anything. The unhurried path looks like this: start with the free tier and test for a few weeks without obligation. As soon as you notice you use the tool every day, take the individual plan. Only consider a local model or a business tier once confidential data or a team come into play.

That way you never pay more than necessary and still win back hours every month.

The outcome

For a Swiss self-employed person, AI realistically costs between zero and thirty francs a month — a fraction of what one hour of your own work is worth. The real question is not whether it pays off, but whether you with care find the entry point that suits your business. That is exactly what a short, no-obligation conversation can help you with.

The messy lead problem

A simple CRM without buying a CRM

Start with a lightweight structure. One spreadsheet, Notion table, or even a simple text file can be enough in the beginning. The goal is to capture every new inquiry in one place with five fields: name, source, summary, next step, and follow-up date.

Then create three clear stages: New, Waiting, and Closed. That alone already removes a surprising amount of mental load.

Where AI actually helps

AI does not need to replace your customer relationship management. It just needs to reduce the repetitive work around it.

  • Summarize inquiries: Turn a long WhatsApp thread or email exchange into a three-line brief.

  2. Use AI to generate a short summary and a first draft reply.

The goal is simple: fewer dropped conversations, clearer follow-ups, and a small system you will actually keep using next month.

Why local models matter here. A self-hosted agent usually still calls a hosted model (Claude, GPT…) over an API. Hermes lets you swap that for an open-weight model running on your own hardware — a valuable option when client data must never leave your premises.

Hosted vs local

The biggest practical decision isn't which agent — it's where it runs and where your data goes. For a Swiss business handling client data, this question usually decides the rest.

6 min read
On this page
The two modelsWhere your data actually goesWhat about the model itself?

The two models

Local (self-hosted)Hosted / cloud SaaS
Data locationStays on your hardwareProcessed on a vendor's servers
SetupYou install & maintain itZero setup, vendor runs it
CostFree software; you pay model/API usageSubscription + usage
ControlFull control, inspectable, extensibleLimited to vendor features
Privacy / DSGEasier to keep client data closeDepends on vendor & data-processing terms
Best forSensitive data, tinkerers, long-term controlSpeed, no maintenance, teams without IT

Both OpenClaw and Hermes are local-first by design — you run the agent on your own machine or server. That's a natural fit for Swiss businesses that want client data to stay under their control.

Where your data actually goes

Under the Swiss Data Protection Act (DSG/nDSG), client data must be handled carefully — which is why a notary, doctor, fiduciary or anyone holding sensitive information should think about this before adopting an agent.

  • The agent itself (the harness that reads your inbox and calls tools) runs on hardware you control.
  • The model (the reasoning brain) usually runs in a vendor's cloud — unless you deliberately run a local model.
  • Your memory and skills (what the agent has learned about you) live on your own machine.

So "local" can mean two things: a local agent (common, easy) or a local model (more work, but nothing sensitive leaves your premises).

What about the model itself?

Even a local agent usually calls a hosted model (like Claude or GPT) over an API. If you want the reasoning local too, you can run an open-weight model on your own hardware — Hermes supports local models natively, and OpenClaw has community adaptations for models like DeepSeek.

A practical note: local is powerful, not mandatory. The sweet spot for many small teams is a self-hosted agent wired to a reputable hosted model, with sensitive documents handled through local tools or models where required. It's a dial, not a switch — and a good setup conversation is the fastest way to find the right setting for your business.

OpenClaw 🦞

OpenClaw is a free, open-source personal assistant that runs on your own computer and lives inside the chat apps you already use — WhatsApp, Telegram, Signal, Discord and more. You message it like a colleague; it acts on your email, calendar and connected services.

What OpenClaw is

OpenClaw was created by Austrian developer Peter Steinberger and launched in November 2025 (first as "Warelay", then briefly "Moltbot") before settling on OpenClaw in January 2026 — with a lobster mascot, Molty 🦞, that became something of an internet phenomenon.

It grew to one of the most-starred repositories on GitHub — close to 400,000 stars — within months. Steinberger has since joined OpenAI, while a non-profit OpenClaw Foundation stewards the project. The point for you: a very active community, rapid improvements, and a tool you can keep and control.

What it does well

💬

Chat-app interface

No separate app to learn — the agent lives inside WhatsApp, Telegram, Signal or Discord.

🧠

Persistent memory

Remembers context, people and preferences across sessions, around the clock.

🛠️

Skills (SKILL.md)

Reusable, shareable procedures for consistent work — with a large community ecosystem.

⏰

Heartbeats & scheduling

Proactive background tasks, reminders and scheduled jobs that run without you asking.

🔌

Deep integrations

Email, calendar, GitHub, 1Password, Beeper, Twilio, X and many more.

📱

Companion apps

Native apps for macOS, Windows and mobile (iOS/Android) to manage the gateway.

How you get it

OpenClaw is installed on a machine you control — a laptop, a small office computer or a server. Installation is a one-liner, followed by a guided onboarding:

Terminal
# Install OpenClaw (installs Node.js and everything else)
curl -fsSL https://openclaw.ai/install.sh | bash

#...or via npm
npm i -g openclaw

# Guided onboarding — meet your lobster
openclaw onboard
You don't have to do this yourself. For most self-employed people and SMEs, the sensible route is to have it set up and secured by someone who knows the terrain — then simply use it from your phone. That's exactly the kind of setup I do for clients.

Security considerations

OpenClaw's power comes from broad access, so treat it with respect:

Prompt injection and third-party skills. Because OpenClaw reads untrusted content (emails, web pages) and can install community skills, security researchers have flagged prompt-injection risks and noted that not every third-party skill is vetted. Install only skills you trust, keep a human approval step, and never let it act on sensitive accounts without review.
  • Microsoft's 2026 partnership brings native Windows support inside Execution Containers, for a more sandboxed experience.
  • Grant the least access each task needs, and review what it did regularly.

Security & data protection

A private, well-configured agent is a genuinely powerful tool. The difference between that and a risk is a handful of habits, not luck. This chapter covers the risks to know and the practices that keep you in control.

8 min read
On this page
The risks to knowSix habits of a safe agentData protection in practice (DSG)

The risks to know

You don't need to be technical to use an agent safely — but it helps to know where the risks live:

🪝

Prompt injection

An email or web page can contain hidden instructions designed to make the model do something you didn't ask for. Treat all untrusted content as data, never commands.

🔓

Over-broad permissions

An agent with access to everything can be tricked or can err. Grant the least access each task needs.

🧩

Third-party skills

Community skills aren't always vetted. Security researchers have found malicious skills that exfiltrate data. Install only what you trust, and review before enabling.

📤

Data leaving your control

Anything sent to a hosted model goes to a third party. Know what leaves, and where it's processed.

Six habits of a safe agent

🔐

Least privilege

Give the minimum access for each task — and start read-only.

👀

Human in the loop

Require approval before sending, deleting, spending or publishing.

🧩

Vet your skills

Only install skills from sources you trust; know what each one does.

🕵️

Secrets stay out of chat

Use the agent's secret storage for keys and passwords, never your prompts.

📋

Log & review

Check what the agent did, and revisit its memory and skills periodically.

🛡️

Sandbox when possible

Run risky or unknown actions in an isolated environment, not your live system.

Data protection in practice (DSG)

  • Keep client data on systems you control; prefer self-hosted agents for sensitive work.
  • Know where the model processes data, and whether you need a data-processing agreement (DPA).
  • Anonymise or minimise before sending anything sensitive to a third-party model.
  • Document what the agent is allowed to access — and keep that list current.

Security done properly

A secure setup — right permissions, approval steps, vetted skills and a clear DSG posture — is exactly what I set up for Swiss clients. It's faster to get right from day one than to fix later.

What is an AI agent?

In one sentence: an AI agent is software that uses a large language model to plan and carry out tasks on its own — and to actually get things done using your tools. It's the difference between asking a question and delegating a job.

6 min read
On this page
An agent acts, a chatbot talksAgents vs chatbots, copilots and automationHow an agent actually worksThe three building blocksWhat that means for your workday

An agent acts, a chatbot talks

If a chatbot is a colleague who gives you an answer when you ask, an agent is a colleague who handles the whole request.

Ask a chatbot "summarise this email thread" and it will produce a summary. Ask an agent the same thing and it will read the thread itself, write the summary, and — if you've asked — draft a reply and file both where they belong. The agent does the reading, deciding and doing; you review the result.

That shift — from answering to acting — is what makes agents useful for the repetitive admin that fills a self-employed person's week: inbox triage, meeting notes, client follow-ups, document drafts.

Agents vs chatbots, copilots and automation

ConceptWhat it doesWho's in charge
ChatbotAnswers questions and generates textYou — every step
CopilotSuggests and assists while you workYou — it augments
Automation / RPARepeats fixed, rule-based steps (no AI)Rules you predefined
AI agentPlans and executes multi-step tasks with tools & memoryIt acts, you approve

The key word is autonomy with oversight: an agent can decide the steps, but a well-configured one still checks in with you before anything irreversible.

How an agent actually works

Under the hood, an agent runs a loop — it keeps repeating these steps until the goal is met or it hands control back to you:

  1. Understand — parse your request into a goal.
  2. Plan — break the goal into concrete steps.
  3. Act — call a tool (search the web, read an email, update a record).
  4. Observe — look at the result and decide the next step.
  5. Report — show you what it did, and wait for approval where needed.
You give a request and an approval; the agent plans, acts through tools, and learns into memory and skills.

The three building blocks

Tool calling

Agents can only do things because they can call tools: the model emits a structured instruction ("read this email", "create this calendar event"), and the agent's runtime executes it. That's the difference between a model that imagines a task and software that performs it.

Memory

Agents keep memory so they don't start from zero every time. Short-term memory holds the current task; long-term memory stores your preferences, people, projects and past decisions. OpenClaw and Hermes both keep this on your own machine, which is why they know you better the longer you use them.

Skills

A skill is a reusable how-to — a packaged procedure the agent loads and follows. Hermes is notable for creating its own skills from experience: when it solves something well once, it saves the approach and reuses it next time. That self-improving loop is its signature strength.

What that means for your workday

Large companies have whole departments for AI. Self-employed people and small teams usually get vague advice and a to-do list they never finish. An agent is different: it's one tool that quietly absorbs the repetitive admin that eats your week — so you can spend it on clients instead of the inbox.

Hébergé vs local

La décision pratique la plus importante n'est pas de savoir quel agent choisir — c'est où il tourne et où vont tes données. Pour une entreprise suisse qui traite des données des clients, cette question décide généralement de tout le reste.

6 min de lecture
Sur cette page
Les deux modèlesOù vont tes données en réalitéEt le modèle lui-même ?

Les deux modèles

Local (auto-hébergé)Hébergé / SaaS cloud
Lieu des donnéesRestent sur ton matérielTraitées sur les serveurs d'un fournisseur
Mise en placeTu l'installes & tu le maintiensZéro installation, le fournisseur s'en occupe
CoûtsLogiciel gratuit; tu paies l'utilisation du modèle/APIAbonnement + utilisation
ContrôleContrôle total, inspectable, extensibleLimité aux fonctionnalités du fournisseur
Protection des données / LPDPlus facile de garder les données des clients chez toiDépend du fournisseur & des conditions de traitement des données
Idéal pourDonnées sensibles, bricoleurs, contrôle à long termeRapidité, aucune maintenance, équipes sans service informatique

OpenClaw et Hermes sont tous deux pensés pour le local en priorité — tu fais tourner l'agent sur ta propre machine ou sur ton serveur. C'est un choix tout naturel pour les entreprises suisses qui veulent garder les données des clients sous leur contrôle.

Où vont tes données en réalité

En vertu de la loi suisse sur la protection des données (LPD/nLPD), les données des clients doivent être traitées avec soin — c'est pourquoi une notaire, un médecin, un fiduciaire ou toute personne détenant des informations sensibles devrait y réfléchir avant d'adopter un agent.

  • L'agent lui-même (le cadre qui lit ta boîte de réception et appelle les outils) tourne sur du matériel que tu contrôles.
  • Le modèle (le cerveau qui raisonne) tourne généralement dans le cloud d'un fournisseur — sauf si tu fais délibérément tourner un modèle local.
  • Ta mémoire et tes compétences (ce que l'agent a appris sur toi) restent sur ta propre machine.

« Local » peut donc signifier deux choses: un agent local (courant, simple) ou un modèle local (plus de travail, mais rien de sensible ne quitte tes locaux).

Et le modèle lui-même ?

Même un agent local appelle généralement un modèle hébergé (comme Claude ou GPT) via une API. Si tu veux aussi le raisonnement en local, tu peux faire tourner un modèle à poids ouverts sur ton propre matériel — Hermes prend en charge les modèles locaux nativement, et OpenClaw propose des adaptations communautaires pour des modèles comme DeepSeek.

Une remarque pratique: le local est puissant, mais pas obligatoire. Le point idéal pour beaucoup de petites équipes, c'est un agent auto-hébergé relié à un modèle hébergé de confiance, avec les documents sensibles traités par des outils ou des modèles locaux si nécessaire. C'est un curseur, pas un interrupteur — et une bonne conversation sur la mise en place est le moyen le plus rapide de trouver le bon réglage pour ta entreprise.

Hermes Agent

Hermes Agent est un agent IA open source de Nous Research, construit autour d'une idée: un agent qui grandit avec toi. Il apprend de l'expérience — enregistrant ce qui fonctionne sous forme de skills réutilisables — et garde une mémoire persistante de qui tu es et de la façon dont tu travailles.

7 min de lecture
Sur cette page
Ce qu'est Hermes AgentCe qu'il fait bienComment l'obtenirSécurité & contrôle
Open source · MITAuto-améliorantPar Nous Research

Ce qu'est Hermes Agent

Sorti en février 2026, Hermes tourne dans ton terminal, une application de bureau native, tes plateformes de messagerie et tes IDE. Il est indépendant des fournisseurs — il fonctionne avec plus de 20 fournisseurs de modèles, y compris les modèles locaux — et il isole dans des sandbox les actions qu'il entreprend pour travailler en toute sécurité.

Sa caractéristique clé est la boucle d'apprentissage: quand Hermes résout bien un problème, il peut enregistrer la démarche comme skill et la réutiliser la fois suivante. Au fil des semaines, il constitue une bibliothèque de la manière dont tourne ton entreprise — une expérience vraiment différente de celle d'un chatbot sans état.

Ce qu'il fait bien

🔄

Boucle d'apprentissage

Crée des skills à partir de l'expérience et les améliore en cours d'utilisation: plus tu l'utilises, plus il devient performant.

🧠

Mémoire persistante

Se souvient de tes préférences, de tes projets et des solutions passées, avec des backends de mémoire interchangeables.

🌐

Passerelle multi-plateformes

Un agent, une mémoire, sur Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp, Signal, e-mail et plus encore.

🖥️

De nombreuses surfaces

CLI, interface de terminal, application de bureau native, tableau de bord web et intégration IDE.

🔀

Indépendant des fournisseurs

Change de modèles et de fournisseurs en plein travail; alterne les identifiants entre plusieurs clés.

🛡️

Sandbox isolée

Cinq backends — local, Docker, SSH, Singularity, Modal — avec durcissement des conteneurs.

Comment l'obtenir

Installe-le avec un installeur shell, puis lance l'assistant de configuration pour choisir ton modèle et ton fournisseur:

Terminal
# macOS / Linux
curl -fsSL https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/install.sh | bash

# Windows (PowerShell)
irm https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/install.ps1 | iex

# Chat interactif / assistant de configuration
hermes
hermes setup

Hermes propose aussi une application de bureau native pour macOS, Windows et Linux, si tu préfères une interface graphique au terminal. Comme avec OpenClaw, la voie la plus pratique pour de nombreuses entreprises est une installation gérée — configurée, isolée et connectée pour toi, puis simplement utilisée depuis ton téléphone ou ton ordinateur.

Sécurité & contrôle

Hermes est conçu en gardant la maîtrise à l'esprit: backends d'exécution en sandbox, masquage des secrets, modes d'approbation et profils qui maintiennent isolés différents contextes (travail, personnel). Le support natif des modèles locaux signifie que tu peux faire tourner le raisonnement sur ton propre matériel si tes exigences de protection des données l'imposent.

Pourquoi les modèles locaux comptent ici. Un agent auto-hébergé fait en général quand même appel à un modèle hébergé (Claude, GPT…) via une API. Hermes te permet de remplacer cela par un modèle open weight tournant sur ton propre matériel — une option précieuse quand les données client ne doivent jamais quitter tes locaux.

Modèles locauxAdaptations communautaires (p. ex. DeepSeek)Prise en charge native, 20+ fournisseurs dont locaux
Applications compagnesmacOS, Windows, iOS, AndroidmacOS, Windows, Linux (bureau)
AmbianceAssistant personnel soigné, énorme communauté 🦞Agent qui s'améliore tout seul et grandit avec toi

Lequel choisir ?

Choisis OpenClaw si…

  • Tu vis dans les apps de chat (WhatsApp/Telegram) et tu veux un assistant soigné, clé en main.
  • Tu apprécies une très grande communauté et de nombreuses compétences prêtes à l'emploi.
  • Tu veux des applications compagnes de premier ordre sur téléphone et sur ordinateur.

Choisis Hermes si…

  • Tu veux un agent qui apprend tes flux de travail et les enregistre comme compétences.
  • Tu as besoin d'un sandboxing précis et d'une flexibilité de fournisseurs (y compris les modèles locaux).
  • Tu es à l'aise dans un terminal ou tu veux une intégration IDE.
La réponse honnête: ce sont des cousins proches — un utilisateur de la première heure a même vu ses agents OpenClaw et Hermes discuter entre eux. Essaie celui qui correspond à tes habitudes quotidiennes; les deux sont gratuits pour expérimenter, et tu peux faire tourner les deux.

Démarrage & exemples

La meilleure façon de juger un agent, c’est de voir ce qu’il ferait dans ta semaine. Voici les schémas qu’on retrouve sans cesse chez les indépendants et les petites équipes suisses — puis un chemin raisonnable vers ton premier agent.

7 min de lecture
Sur cette page
Exemples concrets d’une journée de travail suisseUn chemin de départ raisonnableCe dont tu as besoin

Exemples concrets d’une journée de travail suisse

Tri de la boîte mail et réponses

Avant: 40 e-mails, deux heures de tri, de rédaction et de classement. Après: l’agent rédige les réponses dans ton style, signale ce qui mérite ton regard et classe le reste — tu vérifies en 20 minutes.

Des réunions aux prochaines étapes

Avant: les notes restent dans un carnet et meurent. Après: l’agent transforme les notes en résumé, répartit les prochaines étapes et crée des rappels d’agenda — sans copier-coller.

Relances clients

Avant: « Je devrais relancer ce prospect » est oublié dès vendredi. Après: l’agent suit les points de contact, prépare la relance et te le rappelle au bon moment.

Contexte & recherche

Avant: une heure d’onglets ouverts avant un appel. Après: l’agent rassemble le contexte, prépare une synthèse d’une page et la dépose dans ton canal.

Un chemin de départ raisonnable

  1. Choisis une tâche que tu fais chaque semaine, répétitive et à faible risque (p. ex. résumer une boîte mail partagée).
  2. Choisis un agent — OpenClaw si tu vis dans les applis de chat, Hermes si tu veux la boucle d’apprentissage.
  3. Installe-le sur ta machine ou un petit serveur, et fais la mise en route.
  4. Branche un canal et les outils minimum dont la tâche a besoin.
  5. Configure les validations pour que tout ce qui est sensible attende ton feu vert.
  6. Laisse-le tourner une semaine, vérifie les journaux, puis élargis pas à pas.

Ce dont tu as besoin

  • Une machine pour le faire tourner — un portable ou un petit ordinateur de bureau suffit; un serveur convient aussi.
  • Un fournisseur de modèles ou une clé API (Claude, GPT, DeepSeek…) — ou un modèle local si tu préfères.
  • Les canaux que tu utilises au quotidien — WhatsApp, Telegram, Signal ou l’e-mail.

Tu ne sais pas par où commencer ?

Une mise en place accompagnée fait gagner plus de temps qu’elle n’en coûte. Si tu veux de l’aide pour choisir et configurer un agent adapté à ton flux de travail précis, je me ferai un plaisir d’en discuter avec toi — sans chichi et à ton rythme.

Guide

Qu’est-ce qu’un agent IA ?

En une phrase: un agent IA est un logiciel qui utilise un grand modèle de langage pour planifier et exécuter des tâches tout seul — et pour faire avancer les choses concrètement avec tes outils. C’est la différence entre poser une question et déléguer une tâche.

6 min de lecture
Sur cette page
Un agent agit, un chatbot parleAgents vs chatbots, copilotes et automatisationComment un agent fonctionne vraimentLes trois éléments de baseCe que ça change dans ton quotidien de travail

Un agent agit, un chatbot parle

Si un chatbot est un collègue qui te donne une réponse quand tu lui demandes, un agent est un collègue qui s’occupe de toute la demande.

Demande à un chatbot « résume cette conversation par e-mail » et il te produira un résumé. Demande la même chose à un agent et il lira la conversation lui-même, rédigera le résumé et — si tu le lui as demandé — préparera une réponse et classera les deux au bon endroit. L’agent fait la lecture, la prise de décision et l’exécution; toi, tu vérifies le résultat.

Ce changement — passer de répondre à agir — est ce qui rend les agents utiles pour les tâches administratives répétitives qui remplissent la semaine d’un indépendant: tri des e-mails, notes de réunion, relances clients, brouillons de documents.

Agents vs chatbots, copilotes et automatisation

ConceptCe que ça faitQui décide
ChatbotRépond aux questions et génère du texteToi — à chaque étape
CopiloteSuggère et assiste pendant que tu travaillesToi — il t'assiste
Automatisation / RPARépète des étapes fixes, basées sur des règles (sans IA)Des règles que tu as définies
Agent IAPlanifie et exécute des tâches en plusieurs étapes avec des outils & de la mémoireIl agit, tu valides

Le mot clé, c’est l’autonomie avec supervision: un agent peut décider des étapes, mais un agent bien configuré te demande quand même ton avis avant toute action irréversible.

Comment un agent fonctionne vraiment

Sous le capot, un agent fait tourner une boucle — il répète ces étapes jusqu’à ce que l’objectif soit atteint ou qu’il te rende la main:

  1. Comprendre — transformer ta demande en objectif.
  2. Planifier — découper l’objectif en étapes concrètes.
  3. Agir — appeler un outil (chercher sur le web, lire un e-mail, mettre à jour une fiche).
  4. Observer — regarder le résultat et décider de l’étape suivante.
  5. Rendre compte — te montrer ce qu’il a fait et attendre ta validation quand c’est nécessaire.
Tu donnes une demande et une validation; l’agent planifie, agit via les outils et engrange dans sa mémoire et ses compétences.

Les trois éléments de base

L'appel d'outils

Les agents ne peuvent faire des choses que parce qu’ils savent appeler des outils: le modèle émet une instruction structurée (« lire cet e-mail », « créer cet événement de calendrier »), et le moteur de l’agent l’exécute. C’est la différence entre un modèle qui imagine une tâche et un logiciel qui l’accomplit.

Mémoire

Les agents gardent une mémoire pour ne pas repartir de zéro à chaque fois. La mémoire à court terme contient la tâche en cours; la mémoire à long terme stocke tes préférences, tes contacts, tes projets et tes décisions passées. OpenClaw et Hermes gardent tout ça sur ta propre machine, ce qui fait qu’ils te connaissent de mieux en mieux à mesure que tu les utilises.

Compétences

Une compétence (skill) est un mode d’emploi réutilisable — une procédure prête à l’emploi que l’agent charge et suit. Hermes se distingue en créant ses propres compétences à partir de l’expérience: quand il résout bien quelque chose une fois, il enregistre la méthode et la réutilise la fois suivante. Cette boucle d’auto-amélioration est sa grande force.

Ce que ça change dans ton quotidien de travail

Les grandes entreprises ont des départements entiers consacrés à l’IA. Les indépendants et les petites équipes, eux, reçoivent en général des conseils vagues et une liste de tâches qu’ils ne finissent jamais. Un agent, c’est différent: c’est un seul outil qui absorbe en silence l’administratif répétitif qui dévore ta semaine — pour que tu puisses la consacrer à tes clients au lieu de ta boîte mail.

Sécurité & protection des données

Un agent privé et bien configuré est un outil vraiment puissant. Entre ça et un risque, il n'y a qu'une poignée de réflexes — pas de la chance. Ce chapitre présente les risques à connaître et les pratiques qui te gardent aux commandes.

Lecture: 8 min
Sur cette page
Les risques à connaîtreSix réflexes d'un agent sûrLa protection des données en pratique (LPD)

Les risques à connaître

Pas besoin d'être technique pour utiliser un agent en toute sécurité — mais ça aide de savoir où se cachent les risques:

🪝

Injection de prompt

Un e-mail ou une page web peut contenir des instructions cachées conçues pour faire faire au modèle quelque chose que tu n'as pas demandé. Traite tout contenu non fiable comme des données, jamais comme des commandes.

🔓

Permissions trop larges

Un agent qui a accès à tout peut se faire piéger ou se tromper. Accorde le moins d'accès possible pour chaque tâche.

🧩

Compétences tierces

Les compétences de la communauté ne sont pas toujours vérifiées. Des chercheurs en sécurité ont trouvé des compétences malveillantes qui exfiltrent des données. N'installe que ce qui t'inspire confiance et vérifie avant d'activer.

📤

Des données hors de ton contrôle

Tout ce qui est envoyé à un modèle hébergé passe par un tiers. Sache ce qui part et où c'est traité.

Six réflexes d'un agent sûr

🔐

Moindre privilège

Donne l'accès minimum pour chaque tâche — et commence en lecture seule.

👀

Un humain dans la boucle

Exige une approbation avant d'envoyer, de supprimer, de dépenser ou de publier.

🧩

Vérifie tes compétences

N'installe que des compétences provenant de sources fiables; sache ce que chacune fait.

🕵️

Pas de secrets dans le chat

Utilise le stockage de secrets de l'agent pour les clés et les mots de passe, jamais dans tes prompts.

📋

Journalise et vérifie

Contrôle ce que l'agent a fait et revois régulièrement sa mémoire et ses compétences.

🛡️

Bac à sable si possible

Exécute les actions risquées ou inconnues dans un environnement isolé, pas sur ton système en production.

La protection des données en pratique (LPD)

  • Garde les données des clients sur des systèmes que tu contrôles; privilégie les agents auto-hébergés pour les travaux sensibles.
  • Sache où le modèle traite les données et si tu as besoin d'une convention de traitement des données (DPA).
  • Anonymise ou minimise avant d'envoyer quoi que ce soit de sensible à un modèle tiers.
  • Documente ce à quoi l'agent a le droit d'accéder — et tiens cette liste à jour.

Une sécurité bien faite

Un environnement sécurisé — bons droits, étapes d'approbation, compétences vérifiées et une posture LPD claire — c'est exactement ce que je mets en place pour mes clients suisses. C'est plus rapide de bien faire les choses dès le premier jour que de corriger ensuite.

Cos'è un agente IA?

In una frase: un agente IA è un software che usa un grande modello linguistico per pianificare ed eseguire compiti da solo — e per portare davvero a termine le cose usando i tuoi strumenti. È la differenza tra fare una domanda e delegare un lavoro.

6 min di lettura
In questa pagina
Un agente agisce, un chatbot parlaAgenti vs chatbot, copiloti e automazioneCome funziona davvero un agenteI tre elementi costitutiviCosa significa per la tua giornata lavorativa

Un agente agisce, un chatbot parla

Se un chatbot è un collega che ti dà una risposta quando gliela chiedi, un agente è un collega che gestisce l'intera richiesta.

Chiedi a un chatbot «riassumi questo thread di email» e produrrà un riassunto. Chiedi la stessa cosa a un agente e lui leggerà il thread da solo, scriverà il riassunto e — se gliel'hai chiesto — abbozzerà una risposta e archivierà entrambi dove devono stare. L'agente legge, decide e fa; tu controlli il risultato.

Proprio questo passaggio — dal rispondere all'agire — è ciò che rende gli agenti utili per l'amministrazione ripetitiva che riempie la settimana di un indipendente: smistamento della posta, note di riunione, follow-up con i clienti, bozze di documenti.

Agenti vs chatbot, copiloti e automazione

ConcettoCosa faChi comanda
ChatbotRisponde a domande e genera testoTu — a ogni passo
CopilotaSuggerisce e assiste mentre lavoriTu — lui ti affianca
Automazione / RPARipete passaggi fissi e basati su regole (senza IA)Regole che hai definito tu
Agente IAPianifica ed esegue compiti in più passaggi con strumenti & memoriaLui agisce, tu approvi

La parola chiave è autonomia con supervisione: un agente può decidere i passaggi, ma uno ben configurato si confronta comunque con te prima di qualsiasi cosa irreversibile.

Come funziona davvero un agente

Sotto il cofano, un agente esegue un ciclo — continua a ripetere questi passaggi finché l'obiettivo è raggiunto o ti restituisce il controllo:

  1. Capire — trasforma la tua richiesta in un obiettivo.
  2. Pianificare — scompone l'obiettivo in passaggi concreti.
  3. Agire — chiama uno strumento (cerca sul web, legge un'email, aggiorna un record).
  4. Osservare — guarda il risultato e decide il passo successivo.
  5. Riferire — ti mostra cosa ha fatto e, dove serve, attende la tua approvazione.
Tu dai una richiesta e un'approvazione; l'agente pianifica, agisce tramite strumenti e impara in memoria e skill.

I tre elementi costitutivi

Tool calling

Gli agenti possono fare cose solo perché sanno chiamare strumenti: il modello emette un'istruzione strutturata («leggi questa email», «crea questo evento del calendario») e il runtime dell'agente la esegue. È la differenza tra un modello che immagina un compito e un software che lo esegue.

Memoria

Gli agenti mantengono una memoria per non ripartire da zero ogni volta. La memoria a breve termine conserva il compito attuale; quella a lungo termine archivia le tue preferenze, le persone, i progetti e le decisioni passate. Sia OpenClaw sia Hermes la tengono sulla tua macchina — per questo ti conoscono sempre meglio più a lungo li usi.

Skill

Una skill è un procedimento riutilizzabile — una procedura impacchettata che l'agente carica e segue. Hermes si distingue perché crea le proprie skill dall'esperienza: quando risolve bene qualcosa una volta, salva l'approccio e lo riusa la volta successiva. Questo ciclo di auto-miglioramento è la sua forza distintiva.

Cosa significa per la tua giornata lavorativa

Le grandi aziende hanno interi reparti dedicati all'IA. Gli indipendenti e i piccoli team di solito ricevono consigli vaghi e una lista di cose da fare che non finiscono mai. Un agente è diverso: è un solo strumento che assorbe in silenzio l'amministrazione ripetitiva che ti divora la settimana — così puoi dedicare il tempo ai clienti invece che alla casella di posta.

Hermes Agent

Hermes Agent è un agente IA open source di Nous Research, costruito attorno a un'idea: un agente che cresce con te. Impara dall'esperienza — salvando ciò che funziona come skill riutilizzabili — e mantiene una memoria persistente di chi sei e di come lavori.

7 min di lettura
In questa pagina
Cos'è Hermes AgentIn cosa è bravoCome lo ottieniSicurezza e controllo
Open source · MITSi migliora da soloDi Nous Research

Cos'è Hermes Agent

Rilasciato a febbraio 2026, Hermes gira nel tuo terminale, in un'app desktop nativa, nelle tue piattaforme di messaggistica e negli IDE. È provider-agnostico — funziona con oltre 20 provider di modelli, inclusi modelli locali — e isola (sandbox) le azioni che compie, così può lavorare in sicurezza.

La sua caratteristica distintiva è il ciclo di apprendimento: quando Hermes risolve bene un problema, può salvare l'approccio come skill e riusarlo la volta successiva. Nel giro di settimane costruisce una libreria di come funziona la tua attività — un'esperienza davvero diversa da un chatbot senza memoria.

In cosa è bravo

🔄

Ciclo di apprendimento

Crea skill dall'esperienza e le migliora durante l'uso — più lo usi, più diventa capace.

🧠

Memoria persistente

Ricorda preferenze, progetti e soluzioni passate, con backend di memoria intercambiabili.

🌐

Gateway multipiattaforma

Un agente, una memoria, su Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp, Signal, Email e altro.

🖥️

Molte superfici

CLI, terminale interattivo, app desktop nativa, dashboard web e integrazione negli IDE.

🔀

Provider-agnostico

Cambia modelli e provider a metà flusso; ruota le credenziali su più chiavi.

🛡️

Sandboxing isolato

Cinque backend — locale, Docker, SSH, Singularity, Modal — con hardening dei container.

Come lo ottieni

Installa tramite un installer da shell, poi esegui la procedura guidata per scegliere il modello e il provider:

Terminale
# macOS / Linux
curl -fsSL https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/install.sh | bash

# Windows (PowerShell)
irm https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/install.ps1 | iex

# Chat interattiva / procedura guidata
hermes
hermes setup

Hermes include anche un'app desktop nativa per macOS, Windows e Linux, se preferisci un'interfaccia grafica al terminale. Come con OpenClaw, la strada pratica per molte attività è una configurazione gestita — configurato, isolato e collegato per te, poi usato semplicemente dal telefono o dal desktop.

Sicurezza e controllo

Hermes è costruito con il controllo in mente: backend di esecuzione in sandbox, oscuramento dei segreti, modalità di approvazione e profili che tengono isolati contesti diversi (lavoro, personale). Il supporto nativo ai modelli locali significa che puoi eseguire il ragionamento sul tuo hardware se i tuoi requisiti di protezione dei dati lo richiedono.

Perché i modelli locali contano qui. Un agente self-hosted di solito chiama comunque un modello ospitato (Claude, GPT…) tramite un'API. Hermes ti permette di sostituirlo con un modello a pesi aperti che gira sul tuo hardware — un'opzione preziosa quando i dati dei clienti non devono mai lasciare la tua sede.

OpenClaw 🦞

OpenClaw è un assistente personale gratuito e open source che gira sul tuo computer e vive dentro le app di chat che già usi — WhatsApp, Telegram, Signal, Discord e altre ancora. Gli scrivi come a un collega; lui agisce sulla tua email, sul calendario e sui servizi collegati.

7 min di lettura
In questa pagina
Cos'è OpenClawIn cosa è bravoCome lo ottieniConsiderazioni sulla sicurezza
Open source · MITGira sulla tua macchinaChat-first

Cos'è OpenClaw

OpenClaw è stato creato dallo sviluppatore austriaco Peter Steinberger e lanciato a novembre 2025 (prima come «Warelay», poi per breve «Moltbot») prima di stabilizzarsi su OpenClaw a gennaio 2026 — con una mascotte a forma di aragosta, Molty 🦞, diventata una sorta di fenomeno di internet.

È cresciuto fino a diventare uno dei repository più stellati su GitHub — quasi 400.000 stelle — nel giro di pochi mesi. Steinberger è poi passato a OpenAI, mentre una fondazione no-profit, la OpenClaw Foundation, custodisce il progetto. Il punto per te: una community molto attiva, miglioramenti rapidi e uno strumento che puoi tenere e controllare.

In cosa è bravo

💬

Interfaccia nelle app di chat

Nessuna app separata da imparare — l'agente vive dentro WhatsApp, Telegram, Signal o Discord.

🧠

Memoria persistente

Ricorda contesto, persone e preferenze tra una sessione e l'altra, 24 ore su 24.

🛠️

Skill (SKILL.md)

Procedure riutilizzabili e condivisibili per un lavoro coerente — con un ampio ecosistema di community.

⏰

Heartbeat e pianificazione

Attività proattive in background, promemoria e lavori programmati che girano senza che tu li chieda.

🔌

Integrazioni profonde

Email, calendario, GitHub, 1Password, Beeper, Twilio, X e molte altre.

📱

App companion

App native per macOS, Windows e mobile (iOS/Android) per gestire il gateway.

Come lo ottieni

OpenClaw si installa su una macchina che controlli — un laptop, un piccolo computer da ufficio o un server. L'installazione è un comando unico, seguito da un onboarding guidato:

Terminale
# Installa OpenClaw (installa Node.js e tutto il resto)
curl -fsSL https://openclaw.ai/install.sh | bash

#...oppure via npm
npm i -g openclaw

# Onboarding guidato — conosci la tua aragosta
openclaw onboard
Non devi farlo da solo. Per la maggior parte di indipendenti e PMI, la strada sensata è farlo installare e mettere in sicurezza da qualcuno che conosce il terreno — poi usarlo semplicemente dal telefono. È esattamente il tipo di configurazione che faccio per i clienti.

Considerazioni sulla sicurezza

La potenza di OpenClaw viene da un accesso ampio, quindi trattalo con rispetto:

Prompt injection e skill di terze parti. Poiché OpenClaw legge contenuti non affidabili (email, pagine web) e può installare skill della community, i ricercatori di sicurezza hanno segnalato rischi di prompt injection e notato che non tutte le skill di terze parti sono verificate. Installa solo skill di cui ti fidi, mantieni un passaggio di approvazione umana e non lasciarlo mai agire su account sensibili senza revisione.
  • La partnership 2026 con Microsoft porta il supporto nativo per Windows dentro gli Execution Container, per un'esperienza più sandboxed.
  • Concedi solo l'accesso minimo richiesto da ogni compito e controlla regolarmente cosa ha fatto.

Quale scegliere?

Scegli OpenClaw se…

  • Vivi nelle app di chat (WhatsApp/Telegram) e vuoi un assistente rifinito e pronto all'uso.
  • Ti interessa una community molto ampia e molte skill già pronte.
  • Vuoi app companion di prim'ordine su telefono e desktop.

Scegli Hermes se…

  • Vuoi un agente che impari i tuoi flussi di lavoro e li salvi come skill.
  • Ti serve un sandboxing granulare e flessibilità sui provider (incl. modelli locali).
  • Ti trovi a tuo agio nel terminale o vuoi l'integrazione con un IDE.
La risposta onesta: sono cugini stretti — un primo utilizzatore ha persino visto i suoi agenti OpenClaw e Hermes parlare tra loro. Prova quello che si adatta alle tue abitudini quotidiane; entrambi sono gratis da sperimentare, e puoi usarli tutti e due.
